# Overview



BioPipelines is a Python framework that transforms the complexity of computational protein design into composable, reproducible workflows. Developed at the LOCBP lab (University of Zurich), it provides standardized interfaces to connect over 30 bioinformatics tools — from structure generation with RFdiffusion to sequence design with ProteinMPNN and structure prediction with AlphaFold and Boltz2 — into pipelines that run identically on SLURM clusters and Jupyter notebooks. The framework does not execute computations directly; instead, it generates bash scripts and predicts output file paths, delegating actual execution to your cluster or notebook runtime.

![Ubiquitin inverse folding pipeline](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure1_ubiquitin_pipeline.png?raw=true)

The diagram above illustrates a typical BioPipelines workflow: a PDB structure flows into ProteinMPNN for inverse folding, the designed sequences are validated through AlphaFold refolding and DNA encoding, then filtered by RMSD and pLDDT confidence thresholds. Every arrow represents a **DataStream** — the framework's unified data container — and every box represents a tool invocation defined by a single Python line.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L82), [Docs/index.md](Docs/index.md#L1-L101)

## How BioPipelines Works

At its core, BioPipelines operates on a **declarative pipeline model**. You describe *what* you want to happen — which tools to run, in what order, with which parameters — and the framework figures out *how* to make it happen: generating SLURM batch scripts, managing conda environments, predicting output paths, and wiring data between tools. This is achieved through three foundational abstractions working in concert.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Configuration Phase (Python)"
        A["Pipeline(project, job)"] --> B["Tool A(input=source)"]
        B --> C["Tool B(input=Tool_A.output)"]
        C --> D["Pipeline.__exit__()"]
        D --> E["Generate bash scripts"]
        D --> F["Predict output file paths"]
    end

    subgraph "Execution Phase (Bash)"
        E --> G{"Execution Mode"}
        G -->|"SLURM"| H["sbatch → Cluster nodes"]
        G -->|"On-the-fly"| I["bash → Local/Jupyter"]
        G -->|"Colab"| J["micromamba + bash → Notebook"]
    end

    F --> K["DataStream with predicted files"]
    K --> L["Tables with metrics"]
    K --> M["Plots & Structures"]
```

The **Pipeline** class is the orchestration engine. You open a `with Pipeline(...)` block, instantiate tools inside it, and when the block exits, the framework generates everything needed for execution. Each tool is an instance of a **BaseConfig** subclass — the abstraction layer that normalizes every tool behind a consistent interface regardless of whether it runs RFdiffusion, AlphaFold, or a simple PDB download. Tools communicate through **DataStreams**, lightweight containers that track file paths, IDs, and metadata without loading data into memory.

Sources: [biopipelines/pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L42-L118), [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L22-L70), [biopipelines/datastream.py](biopipelines/datastream.py#L1-L80)

## Two Execution Modes

BioPipelines is designed for two fundamentally different computing environments, and switching between them requires **zero code changes**. The same pipeline script runs unchanged on a high-performance SLURM cluster or interactively in a Jupyter notebook (including Google Colab). This is the framework's central design promise.

| Feature | SLURM Cluster | Jupyter / Colab |
|---|---|---|
| **Submission** | `./submit pipeline.py` or `biopipelines-submit pipeline.py` | Run cells directly in a notebook |
| **Execution** | Generates `sbatch` scripts with resource specs | Tools execute on-the-fly per cell |
| **Environment** | Configured in `config.yaml` under `environments` | Auto-detected via `colab.yaml` + `micromamba` |
| **Resource control** | `Resources(gpu="A100", time="4:00:00", memory="16GB")` | Ignored; uses available notebook resources |
| **Output** | `<user>/BioPipelines/<Project>/<Job_NNN>/` | `./tests/` (or configurable via `local_output`) |
| **Batch support** | Multi-batch with SLURM dependencies | Sequential execution |

In cluster mode, the `./submit` bash script activates the conda environment, runs your Python pipeline to generate SLURM scripts and configuration files, then submits them via `sbatch`. In notebook mode, the `Pipeline` class auto-detects the Jupyter environment and sets `on_the_fly=True`, causing each tool to execute immediately when instantiated. The framework even supports multi-batch pipelines where later batches depend on earlier ones completing successfully.

> [!TIP]
> **Notebook auto-detection** happens at `Pipeline.__init__()` — it inspects the call stack for IPython's `ZMQInteractiveShell` or Google Colab's `_shell` module. You can also force it with the `on_the_fly=True` parameter or the `BIOPIPELINES_OTF=1` environment variable.

Sources: [biopipelines/pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L55-L118), [submit](submit#L1-L80), [run](run#L1-L80), [Docs/index.md](Docs/index.md#L42-L76)

## Tool Ecosystem

The framework integrates over 30 tools spanning the entire computational protein design pipeline, from input preparation to final analysis. Each tool is a Python class that you instantiate with natural parameters — the framework handles environment switching, file path management, and output prediction automatically.

| Category | Tools | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Utilities & Inputs** | `PDB`, `Sequence`, `Ligand`, `CompoundLibrary`, `Load`, `MMseqs2` | Load and prepare input data |
| **Structure Generation** | `RFdiffusion`, `RFdiffusionAllAtom`, `RFdiffusion3`, `BoltzGen` | Generate novel protein backbones and complexes |
| **Sequence Design** | `ProteinMPNN`, `LigandMPNN`, `MutationComposer`, `Mutagenesis`, `Fuse`, `StitchSequences`, `DNAEncoder`, `RBSDesigner` | Design or optimize amino acid sequences |
| **Structure Prediction** | `AlphaFold`, `Boltz2`, `Gnina` | Predict 3D structures from sequences |
| **Analysis** | `Distance`, `Angle`, `DistanceSelector`, `ConformationalChange`, `Contacts`, `PoseBusters`, `PoseChange`, `CABSflex` | Measure and analyze structural properties |
| **Statistics** | `MutationProfiler`, `SequenceMetricCorrelation`, `BayesianAdjuster` | Profile mutations and correlate metrics |
| **Data Management** | `Panda`, `ExtractMetrics`, `Selection` | Filter, merge, sort, and transform result tables |
| **Visualization** | `PyMOL`, `Plot` | Generate molecular visualizations and plots |

The `Panda` tool deserves special mention — it provides pandas-style data operations (`merge`, `filter`, `sort`, `calculate`, `concat`) that work on the result tables produced by other tools, enabling sophisticated filtering without leaving the pipeline. Combined with **Bundle** and **Each** combinatorics, you can systematically explore protein-ligand-structure spaces with minimal code.

![Boltz2 compound library screening](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure3_boltz2_compound_screening.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L82), [biopipelines/__init__.py](biopipelines/__init__.py#L1-L124), [Docs/index.md](Docs/index.md#L14-L30)

## Project Structure

The repository is organized into five functional zones. Understanding this layout helps you navigate the codebase and find what you need quickly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "biopipelines/"
        direction TB
        Core["pipeline.py<br/>datastream.py<br/>base_config.py<br/>combinatorics.py"]
        Tools["alphafold.py<br/>protein_mpnn.py<br/>boltz2.py<br/>rfdiffusion.py<br/>... 30+ tools"]
        Infra["folders.py<br/>config_manager.py<br/>file_paths.py<br/>table_utils.py"]
    end

    subgraph "Configuration"
        config["config.yaml"]
        envs["Environments/*.yaml"]
    end

    subgraph "Examples"
        ex_py["ubiquitin.py<br/>boltz2.py<br/>compound_screening.py<br/>..."]
        ex_nb["notebooks/*.ipynb<br/>(Colab-ready)"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime"
        hs["HelpScripts/<br/>pipe_*.py"]
        ren["Renderers/<br/>streams.py, plots.py<br/>structures.py, tables.py"]
        scripts["submit, run<br/>resubmit"]
    end

    Core --> Tools
    config --> Core
    envs --> scripts
    ex_py --> Core
    ex_nb --> Core
    Tools --> hs
    hs --> Tools
```

- **`biopipelines/`** — The core Python package containing the orchestration engine, all tool classes, and infrastructure modules (folder management, config resolution, table utilities). This is the only directory you `import` from.
- **`config.yaml`** — Central configuration file defining folder paths (with placeholder resolution like `<username>`, `<cwd>`), default conda environments per tool, cluster settings, and Jupyter renderer mappings. This is the file you customize for your environment.
- **`Environments/`** — Conda/mamba environment YAML files for each tool (e.g., `SE3nv.yaml` for RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN, `Boltz2Env.yaml` for Boltz2). Tools are isolated into their own environments and activated automatically at execution time.
- **`ExamplePipelines/`** — Working pipeline scripts (`.py`) and Colab-ready notebooks (`.ipynb`) that demonstrate every major capability. Start here to learn by example.
- **`HelpScripts/`** — Python and shell scripts invoked at execution time by the generated bash scripts. Each `pipe_*.py` handles the runtime details of a specific tool (config generation, output parsing, etc.). You rarely interact with these directly.
- **`Renderers/`** — Display adapters for Jupyter notebooks that render tool outputs inline — molecular structures via py3Dmol, plots, FASTA sequences, and data tables.
- **`submit` / `run`** — CLI entry points for cluster submission and local execution respectively, also available as `biopipelines-submit` and `biopipelines-run` after `pip install`.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L188), [mkdocs.yml](mkdocs.yml#L1-L70), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L24-L30)

## A Complete Pipeline in 30 Lines

The best way to understand BioPipelines is to see it in action. Here is the complete ubiquitin inverse folding pipeline — a real, production-ready workflow that retrieves a PDB structure, designs 10 new sequences, validates them through refolding, and filters by structural fidelity.

```python
from biopipelines.pipeline import *
from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold
from biopipelines.conformational_change import ConformationalChange
from biopipelines.panda import Panda
from biopipelines.dna_encoder import DNAEncoder

with Pipeline(project="Ubiquitin", job="InverseFolding"):
    Resources(gpu="A100", time="4:00:00", memory="16GB")

    # Load input structure from RCSB PDB
    ubiquitin = PDB("4LCD", chain="E")

    # Design 10 sequences via inverse folding
    sequences = ProteinMPNN(structures=ubiquitin,
                            num_sequences=10,
                            soluble_model=True)

    # Predict folded structures
    folded = AlphaFold(proteins=sequences)

    # Encode sequences as DNA for experimental use
    dna = DNAEncoder(sequences=sequences, organism="EC")

    # Measure structural deviation from reference
    conf_change = ConformationalChange(reference_structures=ubiquitin,
                                       target_structures=folded)

    # Filter: keep sequences with RMSD < 1.5Å and pLDDT > 80
    filtered_sequences = Panda(
        tables=[folded.tables.confidence, conf_change.tables.changes],
        operations=[Panda.merge(),
                    Panda.filter("RMSD < 1.5 and plddt > 80")],
        pool=sequences
    )

    # Re-encode filtered sequences as DNA
    dna = DNAEncoder(sequences=filtered_sequences, organism="EC")
```

Notice the key pattern: **each tool receives another tool's output as input**. The `structures=ubiquitin` parameter passes the DataStream from `PDB("4LCD")` directly to `ProteinMPNN`. The framework resolves these references at generation time, predicting the exact output file paths before any computation runs. This is what enables the two-phase execution model — the entire dependency graph is known upfront.

> [!TIP]
> **Tool outputs are accessed via dot notation.** `folded.tables.confidence` gives you a table reference to AlphaFold's confidence metrics, and `conf_change.tables.changes` gives RMSD values. These `TableReference` objects can be passed directly to `Panda` for merging and filtering — no file path manipulation needed.

Sources: [ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py](ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py#L1-L44), [Docs/examples.md](Docs/examples.md#L1-L51)

## What You Can Build

BioPipelines supports a wide range of computational protein design workflows. Here are some of the capabilities demonstrated in the example pipelines and Colab notebooks available in the repository.

| Workflow | Example | Key Tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Inverse Folding** | Ubiquitin sequence redesign | ProteinMPNN → AlphaFold → ConformationalChange → Panda |
| **De Novo Backbone Design** | Kinase LID domain generation | RFdiffusion → ProteinMPNN → AlphaFold → PyMOL |
| **Protein–Ligand Co-folding** | Compound library screening | CompoundLibrary → Boltz2 → Panda → Plot |
| **Iterative Directed Evolution** | 5-cycle binding optimization | LigandMPNN → MutationProfiler → MutationComposer → Boltz2 |
| **Split Sequence Design** | Enzyme redesign near/from ligand | RFdiffusion3 → DistanceSelector → ProteinMPNN + LigandMPNN → StitchSequences → Boltz2 |
| **FRET Biosensor Design** | Linker length optimization | DistanceSelector → Fuse → AlphaFold → Angle → Panda |
| **Combinatorial Screening** | Protein × ligand matrices | Bundle / Each → Boltz2 → Panda |

Every example is available as both a standalone `.py` script and a Colab-ready `.ipynb` notebook, so you can explore them interactively or run them on a cluster.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L36), [Docs/examples.md](Docs/examples.md#L55-L200)

# Quick Start



This page walks you through your first BioPipelines pipeline from zero to a working submission. By the end, you will understand the install → configure → write → run cycle and have a running inverse folding example. For deeper installation details, see [Installation and Environment Setup](3-installation-and-environment-setup); for Colab-specific guidance, see [Google Colab Notebooks Guide](4-google-colab-notebooks-guide).

## How BioPipelines Works at a Glance

BioPipelines does **not** execute bioinformatics tools directly. Instead, you write a declarative Python script that chains tool configurations together. When you run that script, BioPipelines **generates bash scripts and predicts output file paths** — a configuration phase. Those scripts are then either submitted to a SLURM cluster or executed interactively in a Jupyter notebook. This separation is the key architectural idea behind the framework.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Python Pipeline Script"] --> B["BioPipelines Engine"]
    B --> C{"Execution Mode"}
    C -->|"biopipelines-submit"| D["SLURM Cluster"]
    C -->|"biopipelines-run"| E["Local Bash Execution"]
    C -->|"Notebook / Colab"| F["On-the-Fly<br/>(auto-detected)"]
    D --> G["Bash Scripts + Tool Outputs"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["Structures · Sequences · Tables · Plots"]
```

The pipeline script you write has two responsibilities: **declare tool inputs and parameters**, and **connect outputs to downstream inputs**. The framework handles environment switching, dependency ordering, filesystem layout, and SLURM resource management.

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L42-L48), [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L159-L173)

## Step 1 — Install BioPipelines

### Cluster Installation (conda / mamba)

Clone the repository, create the conda environment, and install the package in editable mode. Editable installation means `git pull` updates take effect immediately without reinstalling.

```bash
# 1. Clone and enter the repository
git clone https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines
cd biopipelines

# 2. Create the base environment (contains pyyaml, pandas, ipykernel, etc.)
mamba env create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml
mamba activate biopipelines

# 3. Install in editable mode
pip install -e .

# 4. Register as a Jupyter kernel (optional, for notebooks)
ipython kernel install --user --name biopipelines
```

> [!TIP]
> If your cluster allocates low memory to the default shell (causing `std_alloc` errors during environment creation), run the entire procedure inside an interactive SLURM session: `srun --mem=16GB --time=1:00:00 --pty bash`.

Sources: [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L49-L72), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L37)

### Google Colab Installation

Colab requires no cluster — BioPipelines auto-detects the Colab environment and loads `colab.yaml` instead of `config.yaml`. Tools are installed via `micromamba` into isolated environments. Run these cells at the top of your notebook:

```python
# Cell 1: Install BioPipelines and micromamba
!git clone https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines
%cd biopipelines
!pip install -e ".[all]"
!wget -q https://github.com/mamba-org/micromamba-releases/releases/latest/download/micromamba-linux-64 -O /usr/local/bin/micromamba && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/micromamba
!micromamba create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml -y
```

```python
# Cell 2: Install the specific tools you need (one-time per session)
from biopipelines.pipeline import *
from biopipelines.rfdiffusion import RFdiffusion

with Pipeline("Setup", "install", description="Install tools"):
    RFdiffusion.install()
```

Sources: [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L73-L127), [index.md](Docs/index.md#L1-L101)

## Step 2 — Configure Your Environment

Before running any pipeline, edit `config.yaml` at the repository root to match your system. The two critical sections are:

| Section | Purpose | What to change |
|---------|---------|----------------|
| `folders.base` | Define home, scratch, and group paths | Set `<username>` or hardcode paths |
| `environments` | Map each tool to its conda environment name | Ensure environment names match your system |

```yaml
# config.yaml — key sections to review
folders:
  base:
    home: "/home/<username>"
    data: "<home>/data"
    scratch: "/scratch/<username>"
    group: "/shares/locbp.chem.uzh"     # ← your group share
    biopipelines_output: "<user>/BioPipelines"

cluster:
  env_manager: "mamba"                  # "mamba" or "conda"
  slurm_modules:                        # module load commands for SLURM
    - "miniforge3"
    - "apptainer"
```

Use `bp-config show` to verify the fully resolved configuration after editing:

```bash
bp-config show    # prints all resolved paths and environment names
```

Individual tool models (AlphaFold, RFdiffusion, Boltz2, etc.) must be installed separately. The repository provides an automated installer:

```bash
cd ExamplePipelines
biopipelines-submit install_tools.py
```

Refer to each tool's official documentation if your cluster requires custom adjustments.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L188), [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L556-L585)

## Step 3 — Write Your First Pipeline

A BioPipelines pipeline follows a consistent pattern: **create a context → declare resources → chain tools → let the framework handle execution**. Every tool is a Python class whose constructor defines its inputs and parameters. Outputs are returned as structured objects that you pass directly to the next tool.

Here is the complete inverse folding example from [ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py](ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py):

```python
from biopipelines.pipeline import *
from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold
from biopipelines.conformational_change import ConformationalChange
from biopipelines.panda import Panda
from biopipelines.dna_encoder import DNAEncoder

with Pipeline(project="Ubiquitin", job="InverseFolding"):
    Resources(gpu="A100", time="4:00:00", memory="16GB")

    # Step 1: Fetch a structure from RCSB (chain E of 4LCD)
    ubiquitin = PDB("4LCD", chain="E")

    # Step 2: Design 10 new sequences with ProteinMPNN
    sequences = ProteinMPNN(structures=ubiquitin,
                            num_sequences=10,
                            soluble_model=True)

    # Step 3: Predict folded structures with AlphaFold
    folded = AlphaFold(proteins=sequences)

    # Step 4: Calculate structural deviation from the original
    conf_change = ConformationalChange(reference_structures=ubiquitin,
                                       target_structures=folded)

    # Step 5: Filter — keep only sequences with RMSD < 1.5 Å and pLDDT > 80
    filtered_sequences = Panda(tables=[folded.tables.confidence,
                                       conf_change.tables.changes],
                               operations=[Panda.merge(),
                                           Panda.filter("RMSD < 1.5 and plddt > 80")],
                               pool=sequences)

    # Step 6: Generate optimized DNA coding sequences
    dna = DNAEncoder(sequences=filtered_sequences, organism="EC")
```

![Ubiquitin inverse folding pipeline](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure1_ubiquitin_pipeline.png?raw=true)

Let's break down the key structural elements in this script:

**Pipeline context** — The `with Pipeline(...)` block creates a named, versioned job. The `project` and `job` parameters determine the output folder hierarchy: `<biopipelines_output>/<project>/<job>_001/`. Re-running the same pipeline increments the suffix automatically ([_save_original_pipeline_script](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1361-L1367)).

**Resources()** — Declares SLURM requirements (GPU type, memory, time). When using multiple `Resources()` calls, the pipeline is split into sequential batches where later batches wait for earlier ones to complete ([Resources](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1421-L1449)).

**Tool chaining** — Each tool returns a `ToolOutput` object containing **streams** (file-backed data like structures, sequences, compounds) and **tables** (CSV metadata like confidence scores, affinities). You pass these outputs directly into the next tool's constructor. The framework resolves all paths and dependencies automatically ([_auto_register](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L277-L346)).

**Panda for filtering** — The `Panda` tool provides pandas-style operations (filter, sort, merge, concat). When you pass `pool=sequences`, Panda copies the structures matching filtered IDs into its own output, creating a ready-to-use filtered result ([UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L499-L555)).

Sources: [ubiquitin.py](ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py#L1-L44), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L50-L50), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L913-L987)

## Step 4 — Run the Pipeline

### Option A: Submit to SLURM Cluster

The recommended path for production workloads. BioPipelines generates a bash script and submits it via `sbatch`:

```bash
# From any directory (biopipelines env must be activated)
biopipelines-submit ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py

# Or from the repository root, using the shell script
./submit ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py

# Verbose mode shows full generation output
biopipelines-submit -v ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py
```

You can also submit from a Jupyter notebook:

```bash
biopipelines-submit ExamplePipelines/notebooks/ubiquitin.ipynb
```

### Option B: Run Locally

Execute the generated bash scripts directly on the current machine without SLURM:

```bash
biopipelines-run ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py
./run ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py
```

### Option C: On-the-Fly (Jupyter / Colab)

On-the-fly execution is **automatically enabled** inside Jupyter notebooks and Google Colab. Tools run sequentially as they are added — no `with` block or `Resources()` required. The pipeline context persists across notebook cells:

```python
# Cell 1: First tools execute immediately
Pipeline("Test", "quick_run")
protein = PDB("168L")
rfd = RFdiffusion(pdb=protein, contigs='50-70/A81-140', num_designs=3)
# ← rfd is already complete at this point

# Cell 2: Continue building on previous results
pmpnn = ProteinMPNN(structures=rfd, num_sequences=2)
# ← pmpnn is already complete
```

### Execution Modes at a Glance

| Feature | `biopipelines-submit` | `biopipelines-run` | On-the-Fly (Notebook) |
|---------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| SLURM job scheduling | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Environment auto-switching | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Interactive / step-by-step | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| GPU resource management | ✅ | Manual | Colab-assigned |
| Requires `with` block | ✅ | ✅ | Optional |
| Requires `Resources()` | ✅ | Ignored | Optional |
| Completion check (skip done) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Output location | Config-defined | Config-defined | `./BioPipelines/` |

Sources: [cli.py](biopipelines/cli.py#L99-L106), [submit](submit#L1-L50), [run](run#L1-L50), [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L423-L460)

## Step 5 — Understand the Output

After a pipeline runs, all artifacts are organized in a deterministic folder structure:

```
<biopipelines_output>/<project>/<job>_001/
├── RunTime/                    # Generated execution scripts
│   ├── pipeline.sh             # Main pipeline script
│   ├── 001_PDB.sh              # Per-tool execution scripts
│   ├── 002_ProteinMPNN.sh
│   └── slurm.sh                # SLURM wrapper (cluster mode)
├── Logs/                       # Execution logs
│   ├── 001_PDB.log
│   └── 002_ProteinMPNN.log
├── ToolOutputs/                # Output predictions (JSON metadata)
│   ├── 001_PDB.json
│   └── 002_ProteinMPNN.json
├── 001_PDB/                    # Actual tool outputs
│   ├── .expected_outputs.json
│   └── 4LCD_E.pdb
└── 002_ProteinMPNN/
    ├── .expected_outputs.json
    └── seqs/ ...
```

When things go wrong, check `Logs/<NNN>_<tool>.log` for the relevant tool's stderr and stdout output.

Sources: [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L556-L585)

## Anatomy of a Pipeline Script

Every BioPipelines script, regardless of complexity, is built from four composable ingredients:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Pipeline Script Structure"
        A["1. Imports<br/>from biopipelines.pipeline import *<br/>from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN"]
        B["2. Context + Resources<br/>with Pipeline(project, job):<br/>  Resources(gpu='A100', ...)"]
        C["3. Input Entities<br/>PDB() · Sequence() · Ligand()<br/>CompoundLibrary() · Table()"]
        D["4. Tool Chain<br/>Tool A → Tool B → Tool C<br/>(outputs auto-connect)"]
    end
    A --> B --> C --> D
    D --> E["Bash scripts generated<br/>→ Submitted or executed"]
```

**Input entities** are the starting points for data. They resolve to files and metadata that downstream tools consume:

| Entity | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `PDB` | Fetch structures from local folder or RCSB | `PDB("4LCD", chain="E")` |
| `Sequence` | Define protein/DNA/RNA sequences | `Sequence("MKTVRQ...", ids="my_protein")` |
| `Ligand` | Fetch small molecules from CCD, PubChem, or SMILES | `Ligand("ATP")` |
| `CompoundLibrary` | Create compound collections with optional expansion | `CompoundLibrary({"asp": "CC(=O)O..."})` |
| `Table` | Load existing CSV files for filtering/merging | `Table("/path/to/metrics.csv")` |

> [!TIP]
> For models that accept PDB paths, sequences, or SMILES as parameters, **always use the entity objects** (`PDB`, `Sequence`, `Ligand`) rather than raw strings. This ensures consistent file resolution and ID tracking across the entire pipeline.

Sources: [UserManual.md](Docs/UserManual.md#L223-L329), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1420-L1479)

## More Examples to Explore

The [ExamplePipelines/](ExamplePipelines/) folder contains 20+ ready-to-run pipelines covering the full spectrum of BioPipelines capabilities. Here are the most instructive starting points beyond ubiquitin:

| Example | File | What It Demonstrates |
|---------|------|---------------------|
| **Boltz2 Showcase** | `boltz2.py` | All Boltz2 input modes: sequences, PDB, ligands, DNA, glycosylation, covalent linkages, combinatorics |
| **Compound Screening** | `compound_screening.py` | Protein–DNA–ligand co-folding with `CompoundLibrary` from CDXML, `Bundle`/`Each` combinatorics |
| **Iterative Optimization** | `iterative_binding_optimization.py` | Multi-cycle directed evolution loop with LigandMPNN, MutationProfiler, MutationComposer |
| **RFdiffusion + MPNN + AF2** | `rfd_pmpnn_af2_one_line.py` | De novo backbone generation → sequence design → structure prediction in one pipeline |
| **FRET Biosensor** | `FRET.py` | Linker length optimization with angle-based filtering for a biosensor design |
| **Kinase LID Redesign** | `kinase_LID_redesign.py` | Domain redesign with RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, and conformational analysis |

Each example has a corresponding **results notebook** in `ExamplePipelines/notebooks/` with output rendered inline, and most have an **Open in Colab** badge in the [README](README.md#L10-L20) for zero-setup exploration.

![Boltz2 compound library screening](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure3_boltz2_compound_screening.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L20), [examples.md](Docs/examples.md#L1-L306)

## CLI Commands Reference

BioPipelines installs four command-line entry points when you run `pip install -e .`:

| Command | Alias | Purpose |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `biopipelines-submit` | `bp-submit` | Generate scripts and submit to SLURM |
| `biopipelines-run` | `bp-run` | Generate scripts and execute locally |
| `biopipelines-otf` | `bp-otf` | Submit on-the-fly job to SLURM (runs immediately, survives disconnect) |
| `biopipelines-config` | `bp-config` | Inspect resolved configuration (paths, environments, cluster settings) |

```bash
# Verify your setup
bp-config show         # Full resolved configuration
bp-config folder PDBs  # Check a specific folder path
bp-config env AlphaFold  # Check a specific tool's environment

# Run with verbose output for debugging
bp-submit -v ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py
bp-run -v ExamplePipelines/ubiquitin.py
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L22-L29), [cli.py](biopipelines/cli.py#L5-L10)

# Installation and Environment Setup



This page walks you through setting up BioPipelines from a fresh clone to a fully operational environment — whether you work on an HPC cluster with SLURM, a local Jupyter installation, or Google Colab. BioPipelines uses a **two-layer environment model**: a lightweight base package for the framework itself, and tool-specific environments that are created on demand when you first use each computational tool.

![Ubiquitin inverse folding pipeline: PDB → ProteinMPNN → AlphaFold + DNAEncoder](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure1_ubiquitin_pipeline.png?raw=true)

## Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure your system meets these requirements. BioPipelines targets **Linux** as its primary platform for both cluster and local use, with **Google Colab** as a secondary fully-supported environment.

| Requirement | Details | Verified In |
|---|---|---|
| **Python** | >= 3.10, < 3.13 | [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L10) |
| **Environment manager** | Mamba (recommended) or Conda — Miniforge/Mambaforge preferred | [config.yaml](config.yaml#L155) |
| **Git** | For cloning the repository and tool submodules | [submit](submit#L1) |
| **GPU** (optional) | NVIDIA GPU with CUDA drivers for deep learning tools (RFdiffusion, AlphaFold, Boltz2) | [SE3nv.yaml](Environments/SE3nv.yaml) |
| **SLURM** (optional) | Only needed for cluster job submission | [submit](submit#L1) |

## Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates how BioPipelines organizes its installation across the framework package, configuration, environment files, and tool-specific environments:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Repository Root"
        A["biopipelines/ (Python package)"]
        B["config.yaml (cluster config)"]
        C["colab.yaml (Colab config)"]
        D["Environments/*.yaml"]
        E["submit / run (CLI scripts)"]
        F["ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py"]
    end

    subgraph "ConfigManager (Auto-detection)"
        CM{"Running in Colab?"}
        CM -->|Yes| C
        CM -->|No| B
    end

    subgraph "Environment Layer"
        BP["biopipelines<br/>(base env)"]
        PE["ProteinEnv<br/>(PyMOL, analysis)"]
        SE["SE3nv<br/>(PyTorch, CUDA 11.8)"]
        OT["Tool-specific envs<br/>(Boltz2Env, ligandmpnn_env, …)"]
    end

    A -->|"pip install -e ."| BP
    D -->|"mamba env create"| PE
    D -->|"mamba env create"| SE
    F -->|"install() calls"| OT

    B -->|"folders, environments, cluster"| CM
    E -->|"activates biopipelines env"| BP

    style BP fill:#1a936f,color:#fff
    style PE fill:#88d498,color:#000
    style SE fill:#f6ae2d,color:#000
    style OT fill:#f26419,color:#fff
```

The **ConfigManager** ([biopipelines/config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L61)) acts as a singleton that auto-detects your platform. On Google Colab it loads `colab.yaml`; everywhere else it loads `config.yaml`. This determines where tools are installed, which environments they use, and how SLURM jobs are configured.

## Step 1: Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines.git
cd biopipelines
```

The repository root contains the `config.yaml` (or `colab.yaml`), the `Environments/` directory with environment specifications, and the `submit`/`run` shell scripts at the top level. Your pipeline scripts will live inside this directory or reference it via an absolute path.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L82), [config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L188)

## Step 2: Install the Base BioPipelines Package

The base package provides the framework itself — pipeline orchestration, tool abstractions, data flow management, and configuration handling. It requires no GPU and has minimal dependencies.

```bash
# Create the base conda environment
mamba env create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml
mamba activate biopipelines

# Install the biopipelines package in editable mode
pip install -e .
```

The `biopipelines.yaml` environment ([Environments/biopipelines.yaml](Environments/biopipelines.yaml#L1-L26)) includes: **pandas**, **numpy**, **pyyaml 6.0**, **requests**, **biopython**, **rdkit**, **openbabel**, **ipykernel**, and **openpyxl**. The `pip install -e .` command registers the CLI entry points defined in [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L24-L31):

| CLI Command | Entry Point | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `bp-submit` / `biopipelines-submit` | `biopipelines.cli:submit` | Generate pipeline + submit to SLURM |
| `bp-run` / `biopipelines-run` | `biopipelines.cli:run` | Generate pipeline + run locally |
| `bp-config` / `biopipelines-config` | `biopipelines.cli:config` | Manage configuration |
| `bp-otf` / `biopipelines-otf` | `biopipelines.cli:otf` | On-the-fly SLURM execution with output streaming |

> [!TIP]
> The `submit` and `run` bash scripts at the repository root are thin wrappers that read your `config.yaml` to determine the environment manager, load SLURM modules, activate the `biopipelines` environment, and then execute your pipeline script. You can use either the bash scripts (`./submit pipeline.py`) or the installed CLI commands (`bp-submit pipeline.py`) — they are functionally equivalent.

Sources: [Environments/biopipelines.yaml](Environments/biopipelines.yaml#L1-L26), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L37), [submit](submit#L20-L85), [run](run#L20-L68)

## Step 3: Configure `config.yaml` for Your System

The `config.yaml` at the repository root is the central configuration file. It defines **folder paths** (where tools are installed, where output goes), **environment mappings** (which conda env each tool uses), and **cluster settings** (SLURM modules, environment manager, container executor). You must customize at least the **folders** section for your system.

### Folder Paths

The folder system uses a **placeholder resolution chain**: `base → infrastructure → shared_overrides → repositories → cache → server`. The `<username>` and `<cwd>` placeholders are injected at runtime from the current user and working directory ([config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L188)).

```yaml
folders:
  base:
    home: "/home/<username>"
    data: "<home>/data"
    scratch: "/scratch/<username>"
    group: "/shares/locbp.chem.uzh"      # ← Change to your group path
    user: "<group>/<username>"
    biopipelines: "<cwd>"                # ← Auto-resolved to repo root
    biopipelines_output: "<user>/BioPipelines"
```

Key paths you should review:

| Path Key | Purpose | Typical Customization |
|---|---|---|
| `base.data` | Where tool repositories are cloned | Point to your data storage |
| `base.scratch` | Temporary files during pipeline runs | Your scratch directory |
| `base.group` | Shared resources (cache, containers) | Your research group path |
| `repositories.*` | Per-tool installation directories | Only if you move defaults |

### Cluster Settings

The `cluster` section controls environment manager choice and SLURM behavior ([config.yaml](config.yaml#L148-L167)):

```yaml
cluster:
  env_manager: "mamba"          # "mamba" or "conda"
  container_executor: "apptainer"  # "apptainer" or "singularity"
  slurm_modules:                # Module load commands for SLURM scripts
    - "miniforge3"
    - "apptainer"
```

If you are not on an SLURM cluster, you can set `slurm_modules: []` and use the `./run` script or Jupyter notebooks for local execution.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L188), [biopipelines/config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L88-L132)

## Step 4: Install Computational Tools

BioPipelines provides an **automated installation pipeline** that clones tool repositories and creates their conda environments as SLURM jobs. This is the recommended approach for first-time setup on a cluster.

### Option A: Automated Tool Installation (Recommended)

The `install_tools.py` script ([ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py](ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py#L1-L52)) uses BioPipelines' own pipeline system to install tools. Each `Tool.install()` call adds an installation step that, when submitted, runs the tool's internal installation script (git clone, environment creation, model download).

```python
# ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py
from biopipelines.pipeline import *
from biopipelines.rfdiffusion import RFdiffusion
from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold
from biopipelines.boltz2 import Boltz2

with Pipeline(project="Setup", job="InstallTools"):
    Resources(time="8:00:00", memory="32GB")
    RFdiffusion.install()       # Creates SE3nv, clones repo, downloads weights
    ProteinMPNN.install()       # Clones repo (uses SE3nv from RFdiffusion)
    AlphaFold.install()         # LocalColabFold installation
    Boltz2.install()            # Creates Boltz2Env
```

Run this on a cluster:
```bash
./submit ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py
```

Or run locally:
```bash
./run ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py
```

Comment out tools you don't need to save time. The `install()` method accepts `force_reinstall=True` to redo the full installation ([biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L104-L148)).

### Option B: Manual Environment Creation

If you prefer to create environments individually, use the YAML files in `Environments/`:

```bash
# GPU environment for RFdiffusion + ProteinMPNN (heavyweight: PyTorch + CUDA 11.8 + DGL + PyMOL)
mamba env create -f Environments/SE3nv.yaml
mamba activate SE3nv
pip install -r Environments/SE3nv_pip_requirements.txt

# Lightweight analysis environment (PyMOL, pandas, scipy — no PyTorch)
mamba env create -f Environments/ProteinEnv.yaml

# RBS Designer (ViennaRNA)
mamba env create -f Environments/rbs_designer.yaml
```

### Environment Reference

The following table maps every environment defined in the system to its tools and characteristics. The `environments` section in `config.yaml` ([config.yaml](config.yaml#L80-L144)) links each tool to its required environment:

| Environment | YAML File | Tools | Key Dependencies | GPU Required |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **biopipelines** | [biopipelines.yaml](Environments/biopipelines.yaml) | Load, Fuse, StitchSequences, DNAEncoder, Plot, Panda, PDB, Ligand, Sequence, Distance, DistanceSelector, Gnina, AlphaFold, MMseqs2, CompoundLibrary, BoltzGenMerge, BoltzGenImport | pandas, pyyaml, biopython, rdkit, ipykernel | No |
| **ProteinEnv** | [ProteinEnv.yaml](Environments/ProteinEnv.yaml) | PyMOL, ConformationalChange, Contacts, PoseChange, SASA, Selection | pymol-open-source, scipy, matplotlib | No |
| **SE3nv** | [SE3nv.yaml](Environments/SE3nv.yaml) | RFdiffusion, RFdiffusionAllAtom, ProteinMPNN | pytorch 2.0.1 (CUDA 11.8), DGL, e3nn, pymol | Yes |
| **Boltz2Env** | Created by `Boltz2.install()` | Boltz2 | Boltz-specific packages | Yes |
| **boltzgen** | Created by `BoltzGen.install()` | BoltzGen, BoltzGenMerge, BoltzGenImport | BoltzGen-specific | Yes |
| **ligandmpnn_env** | Created by `LigandMPNN.install()` | LigandMPNN | LigandMPNN-specific | No |
| **MutationEnv** | Created by `MutationProfiler.install()` | MutationComposer, Mutagenesis, MutationProfiler, SequenceMetricCorrelation, BayesianAdjuster | Analysis-specific | No |
| **rbs_designer** | [rbs_designer.yaml](Environments/rbs_designer.yaml) | RBSDesigner | ViennaRNA | No |

> [!TIP]
> When using `./submit` or `./run`, you only need the **biopipelines** environment active. The framework automatically switches to the correct per-tool environment at runtime using the `environments` mapping in `config.yaml`. Each generated SLURM job script or pipeline bash script includes activation commands for the appropriate environment before each tool executes.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L80-L144), [ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py](ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py#L1-L52), [Environments/SE3nv.yaml](Environments/SE3nv.yaml), [Environments/ProteinEnv.yaml](Environments/ProteinEnv.yaml), [Environments/rbs_designer.yaml](Environments/rbs_designer.yaml)

## Step 5: Verify Your Installation

After completing the steps above, verify everything is working with a minimal pipeline:

```python
from biopipelines.pipeline import Pipeline, Resources
from biopipelines.pdb import PDB
from biopipelines.sequence import Sequence

with Pipeline(project="Test", job="Setup"):
    pdb = PDB(pdb_id="1UBQ")        # Fetch ubiquitin from RCSB
    seq = Sequence(structures=pdb)  # Extract sequence
```

Run this test in Jupyter (with `on_the_fly=True` for immediate execution):

```python
with Pipeline(project="Test", job="Setup", on_the_fly=True):
    pdb = PDB(pdb_id="1UBQ")
    seq = Sequence(structures=pdb)
```

If this executes without errors, your base installation and configuration are correct. To test GPU tools, run the [ubiquitin example notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/ubiquitin_results.ipynb).

Sources: [biopipelines/__init__.py](biopipelines/__init__.py#L1-L124), [biopipelines/pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1-L60)

## Google Colab Setup

BioPipelines auto-detects Google Colab by checking for the `google.colab` module import ([biopipelines/config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L73-L82)). When running inside Colab, it automatically loads `colab.yaml` instead of `config.yaml`, which pre-configures paths for `/content/` and uses **micromamba** as the environment manager ([colab.yaml](colab.yaml#L1-L136)).

The setup pattern for Colab notebooks is:

```python
# 1. Clone and install (first cell)
!git clone https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines.git
%cd biopipelines
!pip install -e .

# 2. Run pipeline (subsequent cells)
from biopipelines.pipeline import Pipeline, Resources
from biopipelines.rfdiffusion import RFdiffusion

with Pipeline(project="Test", job="Colab", on_the_fly=True):
    rf = RFdiffusion(...)
```

The provided Colab notebooks in [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/](ExamplePipelines/notebooks/) handle the full setup automatically, including installing micromamba and creating isolated environments per tool. See [Google Colab Notebooks Guide](4-google-colab-notebooks-guide) for the complete walkthrough.

Key differences from cluster setup:

| Aspect | Cluster (config.yaml) | Google Colab (colab.yaml) |
|---|---|---|
| **Environment manager** | `mamba` or `conda` | `micromamba` |
| **Base data path** | `/home/<username>/data` | `/content/data` |
| **Output path** | `<group>/<username>/BioPipelines` | `/content/BioPipelines` |
| **SLURM modules** | System-specific modules | `[]` (none) |
| **Shell scripts** | `./submit` / `./run` | Not used; use `on_the_fly=True` |

Sources: [colab.yaml](colab.yaml#L1-L136), [biopipelines/config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L73-L82)

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `ERROR: biopipelines environment not found` | Base env not created | Run `mamba env create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml && mamba activate biopipelines && pip install -e .` as shown in [run](run#L40-L50) |
| `env_manager not found in config.yaml` | Missing or malformed cluster section | Add `env_manager: "mamba"` under `cluster:` in `config.yaml` ([config.yaml](config.yaml#L148)) |
| `config.yaml missing required section: folders` | Config file corrupted or incomplete | Run `from biopipelines.config_manager import ConfigManager; ConfigManager.pull_config(force=True)` to re-download ([biopipelines/config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L266-L296)) |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'biopipelines'` | Package not installed in active env | Ensure you ran `pip install -e .` while the `biopipelines` conda env is activated |
| Tool fails with CUDA error | Wrong environment or no GPU | Verify GPU availability with `nvidia-smi`; ensure the tool is using its correct environment from the mapping table above |
| Paths not resolving on cluster | `<username>` placeholder not replaced | The `submit`/`run` scripts and `ConfigManager` inject `<username>` at runtime — if using custom scripts, call `ConfigManager()` which handles resolution automatically |

## Summary and Next Steps

After completing these steps, you have: (1) the BioPipelines framework installed as a Python package, (2) a customized `config.yaml` pointing to your filesystem, and (3) tool environments created for the computational tools you need. The framework handles environment switching transparently at runtime, so you never need to manually activate tool-specific environments.

To continue your journey through BioPipelines:

- **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — Write and run your first complete pipeline end-to-end
- **[Google Colab Notebooks Guide](4-google-colab-notebooks-guide)** — Detailed Colab setup with pre-built example notebooks
- **[Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview)** — Understand how the framework orchestrates tools under the hood
- **[Configuration Reference](20-configuration-reference)** — Full documentation of every `config.yaml` option

# Google Colab Notebooks Guide



Google Colab provides a free, GPU-equipped cloud environment that lets you run BioPipelines workflows entirely in the browser — no local installation or HPC cluster required. This guide explains how Colab integration works under the hood, walks you through the universal setup sequence shared by all notebooks, and catalogs every available example notebook with its tool dependencies and biological context.

## How BioPipelines Detects Google Colab

The entire Colab adaptation hinges on a single auto-detection mechanism inside `ConfigManager._get_config_path()`. When the configuration manager loads, it attempts to import `google.colab`. If the import succeeds, it searches the repository root for a file called `colab.yaml` and uses it as the active configuration. If the import fails (meaning you are on a local machine or HPC cluster), it falls back to the standard `config.yaml` instead. This means **no manual environment variable or command-line flag is needed** — cloning the repo into a Colab notebook is sufficient for the framework to reconfigure itself.

Sources: [config_manager.py](/biopipelines/config_manager.py#L41-L63)

## Colab vs. Cluster: Configuration Differences

The two configuration files share identical `environments` and `renderers` sections, but diverge in three critical areas that reflect the constraints of a cloud notebook environment versus an on-premises HPC cluster:

| Aspect | `config.yaml` (Cluster) | `colab.yaml` (Colab) |
|---|---|---|
| **Home directory** | `/home/<username>` | `/root` |
| **Data root** | `<home>/data` | `/content/data` |
| **Scratch space** | `/scratch/<username>` | `/content/scratch` |
| **Output directory** | `<user>/BioPipelines` | `/content/BioPipelines` |
| **Cache** | Group shared storage | `/content/cache` |
| **Environment manager** | `mamba` | `micromamba` |
| **SLURM modules** | `["miniforge3", "apptainer"]` | `[]` (disabled) |
| **Email notifications** | Per-user mapping | `{}` (empty) |
| **GNINA CUDA config** | Custom modules & LD paths | Not configured |

The choice of **micromamba** over mamba is deliberate: micromamba is a lightweight, C++-only binary that installs in seconds without requiring a full conda installation — ideal for the ephemeral Colab runtime. The empty `slurm_modules` list ensures that no cluster-specific module commands are injected into shell scripts when running inside Colab.

Sources: [colab.yaml](/colab.yaml#L1-L136), [config.yaml](/config.yaml#L1-L188)

## Architecture: Colab Execution Flow

The following diagram illustrates how a notebook cell progresses from raw Python code through environment management to a rendered output — all within a single Colab runtime.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Notebook Cell\n(Pipeline Python code)"] --> B{"Is google.colab\nimportable?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["ConfigManager loads\ncolab.yaml"]
    B -- No --> D["ConfigManager loads\nconfig.yaml"]
    C --> E["Resolve folder paths\nto /content/..."]
    D --> F["Resolve folder paths\nto cluster paths"]
    E --> G["Tool.install() triggers\nmicromamba env creation\n+ git clone + model download"]
    F --> H["Tool.install() triggers\nSLURM job submission"]
    G --> I["Pipeline executes\nin Colab kernel\nwith micromamba activation"]
    H --> J["Pipeline executes\non SLURM nodes\nvia submit/run scripts"]
    I --> K["Renderers display\nstructures, plots,\ntables inline"]
    J --> K
```

Sources: [config_manager.py](/biopipelines/config_manager.py#L55-L59), [colab.yaml](/colab.yaml#L127-L136), [config.yaml](/config.yaml#L130-L153)

## The Universal Setup Sequence

Every Colab notebook follows an identical three-cell bootstrap pattern. Understanding what each cell does — and why it is structured that way — will let you adapt any notebook to your own workflow.

### Cell 1: Install BioPipelines and Micromamba

This cell performs four operations in rapid succession. First, it clones the repository into `/content/biopipelines`. Second, it installs the `biopipelines` Python package in editable mode with the `[all]` extra, which pulls `rdkit` alongside core dependencies like `pandas`, `pyyaml`, `biopython`, `ipykernel`, and `py3Dmol`. Third, it downloads the micromamba binary — the fast, standalone conda alternative — and places it at `/usr/local/bin/micromamba`. Fourth, it creates the base `biopipelines` conda environment defined in `Environments/biopipelines.yaml`, which includes `ipykernel` for Jupyter integration and `rdkit` with `openbabel` for chemistry tooling.

```python
# Cell 1: Install BioPipelines and micromamba
!git clone https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines
%cd biopipelines
!pip install -e ".[all]"
!wget -q https://github.com/mamba-org/micromamba-releases/releases/latest/download/micromamba-linux-64 \
    -O /usr/local/bin/micromamba && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/micromamba
!micromamba create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml -y
```

The `[all]` extra is important because `rdkit` is listed as an optional dependency in `pyproject.toml`, yet it is required by tools like `CompoundLibrary`, `Gnina`, and `PoseBusters` that handle molecular structures.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L6-L23), [Environments/biopipelines.yaml](/Environments/biopipelines.yaml#L1-L26)

### Cell 2: Install Required Tools

BioPipelines uses a declarative installation system where each tool class exposes a `_install_script()` method via `BaseConfig.install()`. Inside a `Pipeline` context, calling `Tool.install()` adds an installation step that clones external repositories (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, etc.), creates isolated micromamba environments, and downloads model weights. On Colab, these steps execute directly in the notebook kernel rather than as SLURM jobs.

```python
# Cell 2: Install tools
from biopipelines.pipeline import *
from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold

with Pipeline(project="Setup", job="InstallTools"):
    RFdiffusion.install(weights=[])   # SE3nv environment only, skip large weights
    ProteinMPNN.install()
    AlphaFold.install()
```

The `install()` classmethod accepts a `force_reinstall` flag (default `False`) so that re-running the cell after a runtime restart skips tools that are already present. Individual tools also accept specific keyword arguments — for example, `RFdiffusion.install(weights=[])` creates the shared `SE3nv` conda environment needed by ProteinMPNN but skips the ~4 GB diffusion weights download when you only need sequence design tools.

Sources: [base_config.py](/biopipelines/base_config.py#L61-L115), [install_tools.py](/ExamplePipelines/install_tools.py#L1-L52)

### Cell 3+: Pipeline Code

The remaining cells contain the actual scientific workflow. These cells are **functionally identical** to their cluster counterparts in `ExamplePipelines/*.py` — the same `Pipeline` context, the same tool constructors, the same `Bundle`/`Each` combinatorics. The only difference is execution environment: on Colab, everything runs synchronously in the notebook kernel; on a cluster, steps are dispatched to SLURM via the `submit` and `run` scripts.

> [!TIP]
> The pipeline code in Colab notebooks is a direct copy of the corresponding `.py` script in `ExamplePipelines/`. This means any pipeline that works on the cluster can be pasted into a Colab notebook and will work unchanged — the auto-detection in `ConfigManager` handles all environment differences transparently.

## Available Notebooks

The repository provides six example notebooks, each paired with a pre-executed `_results` version that contains rendered outputs and an "Open in Colab" badge. The pipeline notebooks are interactive templates; the results notebooks serve as proof-of-concept and documentation of expected outputs.

![Ubiquitin inverse folding pipeline](https://github.com/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/Docs/images/figure1_ubiquitin_pipeline.png?raw=true)

### Notebook Overview Table

| Notebook | Biological Task | Key Tools | GPU Required | Approx. Runtime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ubiquitin** | Inverse folding + validation | ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold2, DNAEncoder, Panda | Yes (AlphaFold2) | ~20 min |
| **kinase_LID_redesign** | Backbone design of a kinase domain | RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold2, PyMOL | Yes (RFdiffusion + AF2) | ~30 min |
| **boltz2** | Structure prediction (multi-modal inputs) | Boltz2, CompoundLibrary | Yes (Boltz2) | ~15 min |
| **compound_screening** | SAR screening against protein–DNA | Boltz2, CompoundLibrary, Panda, Plot | Yes (Boltz2) | ~20 min |
| **FRET** | Linker optimization for biosensor | Fuse, Boltz2, Distance, Panda, Plot | Yes (Boltz2) | ~25 min |
| **iterative_binding_optimization** | Directed evolution loop (5 cycles) | Boltz2, LigandMPNN, MutationProfiler, Panda | Yes (Boltz2) | ~60 min |

Sources: [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/ubiquitin.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/ubiquitin.ipynb), [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/kinase_LID_redesign.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/kinase_LID_redesign.ipynb), [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/boltz2.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/boltz2.ipynb), [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/compound_screening.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/compound_screening.ipynb), [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/FRET.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/FRET.ipynb), [ExamplePipelines/notebooks/iterative_binding_optimization.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/iterative_binding_optimization.ipynb)

### Ubiquitin: Inverse Folding

This notebook demonstrates the classic inverse folding workflow. Starting from ubiquitin (PDB `4LCD`, chain E), ProteinMPNN generates 10 sequence variants using its soluble model. AlphaFold2 refolds each variant, and a `Panda` filter retains only sequences with RMSD < 1.5 Å and pLDDT > 80. Passing sequences are then codon-optimised for *E. coli* expression using DNAEncoder.

The results notebook displays inline 3D structure renderings and a confidence table with RMSD and pLDDT columns — the same renderers used on the cluster, now running in the browser via `py3Dmol`.

Sources: [ubiquitin.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/ubiquitin.ipynb)

### Kinase LID Redesign: De Novo Backbone Design

This is the most computationally intensive notebook, combining RFdiffusion for backbone generation with ProteinMPNN for sequence design and AlphaFold2 for validation. It redesigns the LID domain of adenylate kinase (PDB `4AKE`) using an RFdiffusion contig specification that preserves residues 1–117 and 161–214 while generating a 50–70 residue replacement loop. The pipeline then designs sequences on the new backbones, refolds with AlphaFold2, and filters by RMSD on the fixed scaffold regions.

This notebook requires the `SE3nv` environment (created by `RFdiffusion.install()`) and takes the longest to set up due to the RFdiffusion weight download.

Sources: [kinase_LID_redesign.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/kinase_LID_redesign.ipynb)

### Boltz2: Multi-Modal Structure Prediction

The Boltz2 showcase is the most comprehensive single-tool notebook, demonstrating nine distinct input configurations in sequence: direct sequence input, PDB structure input, recycled MSAs, single ligand input, compound library screening, and four combinatorics patterns using `Bundle` and `Each`. It serves as both a tutorial for Boltz2's capabilities and a reference for BioPipelines' combinatorial input system.

Each cell displays a single Boltz2 prediction with its 3D output, making it easy to compare how different inputs affect the predicted structure.

Sources: [boltz2.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/boltz2.ipynb)

### Compound Library Screening

This notebook screens a ChemDraw compound library (supplied as a `.cdxml` file) against the Trp repressor–DNA complex. Boltz2 co-folds each compound with the protein dimer and dsDNA, then predicted affinities are merged with substituent metadata from the compound library. A scatter plot visualizes affinity by substituent group, demonstrating how BioPipelines integrates chemical informatics with structure prediction.

Sources: [compound_screening.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/compound_screening.ipynb)

### FRET Biosensor Design

This notebook optimizes linker lengths for a calcium-responsive FRET biosensor (EBFP–CaM–EYFP fusion). It uses `Fuse` with `linker_lengths=["0-3", "0-3"]` to generate variants with GSG linkers of varying length, then predicts both apo and calcium-bound (holo) structures with Boltz2. Chromophore distances are computed with `Distance`, converted to FRET efficiencies using the Förster equation, and visualized with bar charts showing apo vs. holo efficiency and the calcium-induced ΔFRET.

Sources: [FRET.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/FRET.ipynb)

### Iterative Binding Optimization

This notebook implements a directed evolution loop: starting from the NocT protein (PDB `5OT9`) with Histopine as ligand, it runs 5 cycles of pocket residue identification, LigandMPNN variant generation (1000 sequences/cycle), mutation frequency profiling, and Boltz2 binding affinity evaluation. Each cycle keeps only the best candidate, demonstrating how BioPipelines can express iterative optimization loops with standard Python `for` syntax inside a single `Pipeline` context.

Sources: [iterative_binding_optimization.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/iterative_binding_optimization.ipynb)

## Colab-Specific Dependencies

BioPipelines includes a dedicated requirements file for the `SE3nv` environment on Colab. While the cluster uses a full conda environment specification, the Colab version leverages the fact that PyTorch, numpy, and scipy are pre-installed in Colab's base runtime, listing only the additional packages that `RFdiffusion` and `ProteinMPNN` need beyond what Colab already provides.

The base `biopipelines` environment (`Environments/biopipelines.yaml`) explicitly includes `ipykernel`, which is critical for Colab: it enables the Jupyter kernel to communicate with the notebook frontend, and it is loaded by tools that need the `biopipelines` conda environment when running pipeline steps.

Sources: [SE3nv_colab_requirements.txt](/Environments/SE3nv_colab_requirements.txt#L1-L26), [Environments/biopipelines.yaml](/Environments/biopipelines.yaml#L13-L25)

## Troubleshooting Common Colab Issues

| Problem | Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| **Runtime disconnect during tool install** | Colab sessions timeout after ~90 min of inactivity or ~12 h total | Use "Connect to hosted runtime" with a Colab Pro/Pro+ session for longer runtimes; save outputs with `download()` frequently |
| **`ContentTooShortError` on Boltz2 weight download** | Interrupted network transfer leaves corrupt checkpoint files | Delete cached files: `!find ~/.boltz -name "*.ckpt" -delete` and rerun |
| **CUDA out of memory** | Boltz2 or RFdiffusion exceeds T4 GPU memory (16 GB) | Reduce `num_designs` or `num_sequences`; use a runtime with an A100 GPU if available |
| **micromamba not found after restart** | Colab runtime reset clears `/usr/local/bin` | Re-run Cell 1 — the install cell is idempotent |
| **`google.colab` import fails but colab.yaml is needed** | Custom Jupyter environment that is not Colab | Manually set environment or copy `colab.yaml` to `config.yaml` |

Sources: [boltz2.ipynb](/ExamplePipelines/notebooks/boltz2.ipynb), [colab.yaml](/colab.yaml#L1-L5)

> [!TIP]
> Colab runtimes are ephemeral. Any downloaded model weights, created environments, or generated outputs are lost when the runtime disconnects. For long-running iterative pipelines (like the binding optimization notebook), consider downloading intermediate results to your local machine at each cycle using the `download()` method available on pipeline outputs.
