| `msas` | `StandardizedOutput` | Tool output containing an `msas` stream |
| `convert` | `str` | Target format: `"a3m"` or `"csv"` |

The tool reads from the upstream `msas` table and delegates conversion to `pipe_msa.py`, writing converted files to an `MSAs/` subdirectory with an updated map table. Validation warns (rather than errors) if the input format already matches the target — files are simply copied in that case ([msa.py#L95-L100](/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/biopipelines/msa.py#L95-L100)).

### MSA Format Compatibility

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    AF[AlphaFold] --"MSAs in A3M"--> MSA1[MSA convert='csv']
    MSA1 --"MSAs in CSV"--> BZ_IN[Boltz2 msas=]
    
    BZ_OUT[Boltz2 output] --"MSAs in CSV"--> MSA2[MSA convert='a3m']
    MSA2 --"MSAs in A3M"--> AF2[AlphaFold msas=]
```

Sources: [msa.py](/locbp-uzh/biopipelines/blob/main/biopipelines/msa.py#L86-L100)

> [!TIP]
> AlphaFold performs a strict format check on incoming MSAs. Even if you convert Boltz2 CSV to A3M via `MSA(boltz_result, convert="a3m")`, ColabFold may still reject the files if they lack expected header metadata and re-query the MSA server. For reliable recycling, pass AlphaFold-generated A3M files back to a subsequent AlphaFold run, or Boltz2-generated CSV files back to Boltz2.

## Cross-Tool Pipeline Patterns

The three prediction tools are designed to compose into end-to-end workflows. Below are the most common architectural patterns observed in the example pipelines:

### Sequence-to-Structure-to-Docking Pipeline

This three-stage pattern is the bread-and-butter of computational drug design workflows:

```python
from biopipelines.protein_mpnn import ProteinMPNN
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold
from biopipelines.boltz2 import Boltz2
from biopipelines.gnina import Gnina
from biopipelines.compound_library import CompoundLibrary

# Stage 1: Design sequences → fold with AlphaFold
sequences = ProteinMPNN(structures=target, num_sequences=20)
folded = AlphaFold(proteins=sequences, num_relax=1)

# Stage 2: Predict protein-ligand complexes with Boltz2
compounds = CompoundLibrary({"aspirin": "CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O"})
complexes = Boltz2(proteins=folded, ligands=compounds)

# Stage 3: Refine poses with Gnina
docked = Gnina(structures=complexes, compounds=compounds, num_runs=10)
```

### Boltz2 Apo-then-Holo with MSA Recycling

Boltz2 can first predict apo structures, then recycle the MSAs for holo (bound) predictions, saving significant computation on MSA generation:

```python
# Apo prediction (generates MSAs as side effect)
apo = Boltz2(proteins=sequences)

# Holo prediction reuses the apo MSAs
holo = Boltz2(proteins=sequences, ligands="CCO", msas=apo)
```

### AlphaFold → Boltz2 via MSA Conversion

To recycle MSAs from AlphaFold into Boltz2, the CSV conversion is required:

```python
from biopipelines.alphafold import AlphaFold
from biopipelines.boltz2 import Boltz2
from biopipelines.msa import MSA

folded = AlphaFold(proteins=sequences)
msas_csv = MSA(folded, convert="csv")  # A3M → CSV for Boltz2
holo = Boltz2(proteins=sequences, ligands=compounds, msas=msas_csv)
```


# Analysis and Filtering Tools



Analysis and filtering tools transform raw structural predictions and sequence designs into actionable, quantitative decisions. They form the **evaluative backbone** of every biopipelines workflow — bridging the gap between generative tools like RFdiffusion or Boltz2 and the downstream sequence optimization loop. Every tool in this category follows the [BaseConfig](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer) abstraction, meaning they share a uniform interface for input configuration, script generation, and output table production that integrates seamlessly with the [Two-Phase Execution Model](9-two-phase-execution-model).

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Generative["Generative Tools"]
        RF["RFdiffusion"]
        B2["Boltz2"]
        PM["ProteinMPNN"]
    end

    subgraph Analysis["Structural Analysis"]
        Dist["Distance"]
        Ang["Angle"]
        Cont["Contacts"]
        SASA["SASA"]
        CC["ConformationalChange"]
        PC["PoseChange"]
        PB["PoseBusters"]
        DS["DistanceSelector"]
        CF["CABSflex"]
    end

    subgraph Filtering["Filtering & Transformation"]
        Sel["Selection"]
        Pand["Panda"]
        RM["ReMap"]
    end

    subgraph Stats["Mutation Statistics"]
        MP["MutationProfiler"]
        SMC["SequenceMetricCorrelation"]
        BA["BayesianAdjuster"]
        MC["MutationComposer"]
    end

    subgraph Export["Data Export"]
        EM["ExtractMetrics"]
    end

    RF --> B2
    B2 --> Dist
    B2 --> Ang
    B2 --> Cont
    B2 --> PC
    B2 --> PB
    B2 --> DS
    PM --> CC
    CC --> Pand
    PC --> Pand
    PB --> Pand
    DS --> Sel
    Sel --> PM
    Dist --> Pand
    Ang --> Pand
    Cont --> Pand
    Pand --> EM
    MP --> SMC
    SMC --> BA
    BA --> MC
    MC --> PM
    Pand --> RM

    style Analysis fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196f3,color:#0d47a1
    style Filtering fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ff9800,color:#e65100
    style Stats fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#9c27b0,color:#4a148c
```

The architecture above reveals three functional strata. **Structural analysis tools** extract geometric and physicochemical metrics from predicted complexes — distances, angles, contact maps, RMSD values. **Filtering and transformation tools** then act on the resulting tables to select, sort, merge, and reshape data. Finally, **mutation statistics tools** close the feedback loop by correlating sequence mutations with performance metrics, producing frequency-adjusted inputs for the next design cycle. All outputs propagate through the [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container) and are referenceable via [Table Reference and Provenance](16-table-reference-and-provenance).

## Structural Metric Extraction

Structural metric tools answer a single fundamental question: *how good are the predicted structures?* They accept a `StandardizedOutput` from any upstream tool, compute geometric measurements using PyMOL's internal engine, and emit tables that downstream filtering tools consume. The selection syntax is shared across Distance, Angle, and Contacts — using PyMOL-style selectors like `'10.CA'` for specific atoms, `'LIG.C1'` for ligand atoms, and `'D in IGDWG'` for contextual residue matching.

Sources: [distance.py](biopipelines/distance.py#L5-L11), [angle.py](biopipelines/angle.py#L5-L16), [contacts.py](biopipelines/contacts.py#L5-L10)

### Distance

The `Distance` tool measures inter-atomic or atom-to-residue distances across an entire structure set. It is the workhorse metric for validating ligand binding proximity — answering questions like "is the catalytic chlorine within 3 Å of the binding pocket?" The tool operates through a generated HelpScript ([pipe_distance.py](HelpScripts/pipe_distance.py)) that loads each structure and computes distances at runtime.

Four methods are available, each answering a different structural question:

| Method | Computation | Use Case |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| `min` | Closest atom pair | Ligand binding proximity |
| `max` | Farthest atom pair | Pocket dimension estimation |
| `mean` | Average across all pairs | Bulk interaction strength |
| `closest` | Centroid-to-closest | Region-level proximity |

The output table contains one row per input structure, with the computed distance in the specified unit. When a selection resolves to multiple atoms (e.g., `'D in IGDWG'` matches several aspartates), the method determines how to aggregate. The `metric_name` parameter controls the column label, which becomes critical when multiple Distance instances feed into a Panda merge for multi-dimensional filtering.

```python
from biopipelines.distance import Distance

# Validate chlorine positioning relative to binding motif
chlorine_dist = Distance(
    structures=boltz,
    atom="LIG.Cl",
    residue="D in IGDWG",
    method="min",
    metric_name="chlorine_distance"
)
```

Sources: [distance.py](biopipelines/distance.py#L57-L65), [distance.py](biopipelines/distance.py#L141-L155)

### Angle

The `Angle` tool is more expressive than Distance, supporting three distinct geometric modes determined by the shape of the `atoms` tuple. This polymorphic design — where input structure drives behavior — is a distinctive pattern in biopipelines tool architecture. The `_parse_atoms` static method inspects tuple nesting to classify the mode, then serializes the flat selection list to JSON for the HelpScript ([pipe_angle.py](HelpScripts/pipe_angle.py)).

| Mode | Tuple Shape | Geometric Meaning | Range |
|------|-------------|-------------------|-------|
| Bond angle | `(a, o, b)` | Angle at vertex *o* between arms *a–o–b* | 0–180° |
| Torsion | `(a, x₁, x₂, b)` | Dihedral angle around axis *x₁–x₂* | −180° to 180° |
| Vector | `((a₁, a₂), (b₁, b₂))` | Angle between direction vectors | 0–180° |

The vector mode deserves special attention: it measures the angle between two directed segments, making it ideal for quantifying relative domain orientations (e.g., helix packing angles). When used with `unit="radians"`, the output integrates directly into Panda's `calculate` expressions via `cos()` and `sin()` — enabling FRET efficiency calculations through the Förster equation.

> [!TIP]
> Angle supports negative residue indexing (`'-1.C'` for the C-terminus carbon) and contextual matching (`'D in IGDWG'`). When a contextual match resolves to multiple atoms, centroids are computed automatically. This makes backbone dihedral analysis robust across homologous structures with minor length variations.

Sources: [angle.py](biopipelines/angle.py#L55-L58), [angle.py](biopipelines/angle.py#L139-L175), [angle.py](biopipelines/angle.py#L73-L78)

### Contacts

The `Contacts` tool shifts from point measurements to region-level analysis. Rather than a single atom pair, it evaluates **every residue** in a selection against the ligand, producing per-residue distance statistics and a contact count (residues within the threshold). The output includes `min_distance`, `max_distance`, `mean_distance`, and a `sum_distances_sqrt_normalized` column — the latter dividing total distances by √(residue count) to penalize loose, diffuse contacts.

The `selections` parameter accepts either a string (`'10-20+30-40'`) or a table reference from DistanceSelector, enabling dynamic, structure-aware contact analysis. When `selections` is `None`, all protein residues are evaluated against the ligand.

Sources: [contacts.py](biopipelines/contacts.py#L62-L69), [contacts.py](biopipelines/contacts.py#L105-L109)

### SASA

The `SASA` tool computes **delta solvent accessible surface area** — the difference between ligand SASA alone and ligand SASA in complex. This metric directly quantifies how much of the ligand surface is buried by protein binding: `delta_SASA = SASA_ligand_alone − SASA_ligand_in_complex`. It runs in the `biopipelines` environment using PyMOL's built-in SASA calculation with configurable dot density. The output table provides a single numeric score per structure, ideal for ranking binding modes by buried surface area.

Sources: [sasa.py](biopipelines/sasa.py#L5-L13), [sasa.py](biopipelines/sasa.py#L58-L63)

## Structural Comparison

Structural comparison tools answer a different class of question: *how much did the structure change?* Whether comparing a designed model to an experimental reference, or evaluating conformational variability across an ensemble, these tools produce RMSD-based metrics that quantify structural fidelity.

Sources: [conformational_change.py](biopipelines/conformational_change.py#L5-L10), [pose_change.py](biopipelines/pose_change.py#L5-L10)

### ConformationalChange

`ConformationalChange` aligns two structure sets using PyMOL and reports the per-structure RMSD. The `alignment` parameter selects the alignment algorithm — `align` for sequence-similar structures (>50% identity), `super` for a different minimization strategy, and `cealign` for sequence-divergent structures using combinatorial extension. The `atoms` parameter controls granularity: `"CA"` for backbone-only, `"backbone"` for CA+C+N+O, `"all"` for every atom, or custom combinations like `"CA+CB"`.

The `selection` parameter restricts analysis to specific residue ranges (e.g., `'10-50'`), enabling targeted RMSD evaluation of redesigned loops or binding interfaces while ignoring flexible termini. A table reference can also be passed, allowing dynamic selection from upstream tools.

Sources: [conformational_change.py](biopipelines/conformational_change.py#L63-L69), [conformational_change.py](biopipelines/conformational_change.py#L125-L131)

### PoseChange

`PoseChange` specializes in **ligand pose validation** — aligning protein structures then measuring ligand RMSD and centroid distance. It automatically excludes the ligand from alignment (`"not resn {reference_ligand}"`), ensuring that protein alignment is independent of the ligand pose being evaluated. This makes it the gold standard for answering "does my designed structure reproduce the crystallographic binding pose?"

The output includes `ligand_rmsd` (post-alignment ligand RMSD), `centroid_distance` (spatial displacement), and `alignment_rmsd` (protein fit quality). A typical filtering threshold is `ligand_rmsd < 2.0 Å`, though stricter criteria may apply depending on the application.

Sources: [pose_change.py](biopipelines/pose_change.py#L61-L68), [pose_change.py](biopipelines/pose_change.py#L111-L113)

### PoseBusters

`PoseBusters` provides comprehensive **pose sanity checking** that goes beyond geometric comparison. Based on Buttenschoen et al. (2024), it validates generated poses against chemical and structural plausibility criteria: bond lengths, bond angles, internal steric clashes, aromatic ring flatness, double bond flatness, internal energy, volume overlap with protein, and minimum distance to protein. It runs in a dedicated `posebusters` conda environment with Python 3.10.

Two modes are supported: `dock` (standalone validation) and `redock` (adds RMSD comparison against a reference ligand). The output table contains boolean pass/fail columns for each check, plus an `all_pass` aggregate column. A common pattern is filtering on `all_pass == True` to eliminate chemically implausible poses before further analysis.

Sources: [posebusters.py](biopipelines/posebusters.py#L5-L16), [posebusters.py](biopipelines/posebusters.py#L92-L100)

### CABSflex

`CABSflex` provides **fast coarse-grained flexibility simulation** using Monte Carlo sampling. Unlike the comparison tools above, it generates new structural data — conformational ensembles with per-residue RMSF profiles. It operates in a dedicated `CABSflex` conda environment (Python 2.7) and optionally rebuilds models to all-atom representation using MODELLER (requires academic license). The output includes ensemble structures, SVG diagnostic plots, and a merged RMSF table across all input structures.

Sources: [cabsflex.py](Docs/Tool/Analysis.md#L399-L458)

## Selection and Proximity Tools

Selection tools bridge structural analysis and sequence design by converting geometric criteria into position specifications that downstream tools consume. They answer the question: *which residues matter?*

Sources: [distance_selector.py](biopipelines/distance_selector.py#L5-L10), [selection.py](biopipelines/selection.py#L5-L26)

### DistanceSelector

`DistanceSelector` identifies residues within a cutoff distance from a reference ligand, outputting PyMOL-formatted selection strings in two columns: `within` (residues inside the cutoff) and `beyond` (residues outside). The `reference_type` parameter supports `"ligand"`, `"atoms"`, and `"residues"` as reference sources. The `restrict_to` parameter further constrains the selection to specific chains or residue ranges.

The output table is directly consumable by ProteinMPNN's `fixed_positions` parameter and by the `Selection` tool for further manipulation.

Sources: [distance_selector.py](biopipelines/distance_selector.py#L51-L60), [distance_selector.py](biopipelines/distance_selector.py#L115-L117)

### Selection

`Selection` provides a **composable, operation-based API** for manipulating PyMOL selection strings. Operations are applied left-to-right to a running selection set, using lightweight `SelectionOp` descriptors. This functional composition pattern — where operations are first-class objects chained through positional arguments — is unique to Selection among biopipelines tools.

| Operation | Effect | Structure-Aware? |
|-----------|--------|-------------------|
| `add(*refs)` | Union of referenced columns | No |
| `subtract(*refs)` | Remove referenced residues | No |
| `expand(n)` | Add *n* residues on each side | Yes |
| `shrink(n)` | Remove *n* residues from each side | Yes |
| `shift(n)` | Translate all intervals by *n* | Yes |
| `invert()` | Select complement | Yes |

Structure-aware operations (`expand`, `shrink`, `shift`, `invert`) require a `structures` parameter because they need to know the total residue count and chain boundaries. A common pattern is combining DistanceSelector output with `expand` to create a buffer zone around the binding pocket for fixed-position design.

```python
from biopipelines.selection import Selection

# Expand binding pocket by 2 residues for fixed-position design
expanded = Selection(
    Selection.add(distances.tables.selections.within),
    Selection.expand(2),
    structures=boltz
)
```

Sources: [selection.py](biopipelines/selection.py#L108-L129), [selection.py](biopipelines/selection.py#L134-L137)

## Table Filtering and Transformation with Panda

`Panda` is the **central filtering engine** of biopipelines — a unified, operations-based tool that replaces six legacy tools (Filter, Rank, SelectBest, MergeTables, ConcatenateTables, SliceTable). It accepts tables from any upstream tool, applies a chain of `Operation` objects, and optionally propagates filtered IDs back to associated structure and sequence streams via the `pool` mechanism.

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L5-L11), [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L53-L53)

### Operation Architecture

Each Panda operation is a lightweight `Operation` dataclass with a `type` string and a `params` dictionary. Operations are created via static factory methods on the Panda class and serialized to JSON for the HelpScript ([pipe_panda.py](HelpScripts/pipe_panda.py)). The `_validate_operations` method enforces compatibility — for instance, `merge` requires multiple input tables, while `filter` requires exactly one.

The following table groups operations by their primary function:

| Category | Operation | Key Parameters |
|----------|-----------|----------------|
| **Row selection** | `filter`, `head`, `tail`, `sample`, `drop_duplicates` | Expression string, counts, random state |
| **Ordering** | `sort`, `rank` | Column name(s), ascending flag |
| **Reshaping** | `select_columns`, `drop_columns`, `rename`, `fillna` | Column lists, mappings |
| **Computation** | `calculate` | Dict of `{name: expression}` |
| **Combining** | `merge`, `concat` | Join keys, prefixes, fill values |
| **Aggregation** | `groupby`, `average_by_source`, `pivot`, `melt` | Group columns, aggregation functions |

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L30-L50), [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L118-L400)

### Filtering with Pool Propagation

The `pool` parameter is what makes Panda a true filtering tool rather than just a table transformer. When `pool` is set to a `StandardizedOutput`, Panda tracks which IDs pass the operation chain and creates a filtered output containing only the matching structures, sequences, and compounds. The `rename` parameter additionally renumbers IDs (`"best"` → `best_1`, `best_2`, ...) for clean downstream reference.

```python
from biopipelines.panda import Panda

# Select top-5 structures by confidence, propagate to streams
best = Panda(
    tables=boltz.tables.confidence,
    operations=[
        Panda.sort("confidence_score", ascending=False),
        Panda.head(5)
    ],
    rename="best",
    pool=boltz
)
# best.streams.structures now contains only the 5 best PDBs
```

> [!TIP]
> Panda's `calculate` operation supports mathematical functions (`cos`, `sin`, `sqrt`, `log`, `exp`, `radians`, `degrees`, `pi`) and allows expressions that reference columns defined earlier in the same `calculate` dict. This enables complex derived metrics like FRET efficiency in a single operation chain, without intermediate tables.

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L480-L487), [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L544-L558), [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L289-L315)

### Multi-Table Workflows

Panda's `merge` and `concat` operations enable sophisticated multi-table analysis. `merge` joins tables on biopipelines ID matching (when `on=None`) or on explicit columns, with optional prefixes to disambiguate shared column names. `concat` stacks tables vertically with a `source_table` column tracking provenance. Multi-pool selection — passing multiple `StandardizedOutput` objects to `pool` — allows selecting the best candidate across multiple design cycles.

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L335-L365), [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L366-L385)

## Mutation Analysis Pipeline

The mutation analysis pipeline is a three-stage feedback system that connects sequence diversity with quantitative performance metrics. It enables **data-driven sequence optimization** by learning which mutations improve (or degrade) binding affinity, stability, or any other measurable property.

Sources: [mutation_profiler.py](biopipelines/mutation_profiler.py#L5-L11), [Docs/Tool/Statistics.md](Docs/Tool/Statistics.md#L1-L194)

### Stage 1: MutationProfiler

`MutationProfiler` takes original and mutant sequences, identifies mutations at each position, and computes amino acid frequency distributions. It outputs four tables: `profile` (per-position summary), `mutations` (mutation type breakdown), `absolute_frequencies`, and `relative_frequencies`. Visualization outputs include sequence logos in both SVG and PNG formats, using either a colorblind-friendly `"okabe-ito"` palette or a property-based `"standard"` palette. It runs in a lightweight `MutationEnv` environment (seaborn, matplotlib, pandas, logomaker, scipy).

Sources: [mutation_profiler.py](biopipelines/mutation_profiler.py#L90-L97), [mutation_profiler.py](biopipelines/mutation_profiler.py#L216-L266)

### Stage 2: SequenceMetricCorrelation

`SequenceMetricCorrelation` quantifies how specific mutations affect a chosen metric using Cohen's d-like effect sizes. It computes two correlation tables: 1D (position-level: does *any* mutation at position *i* affect the metric?) and 2D (amino acid-specific: does substituting to *aa* at position *i* improve the metric?). The 2D correlation table is the critical output — it maps directly to the frequency tables from MutationProfiler, enabling per-position, per-amino-acid effect quantification.

The formulas use standardized effect sizes with pooled variance estimates:

```
c(i, aa) = (m̄ᵢ,ₐₐ − m̄ᵢ,¬ₐₐ) / √(s²ᵢ,ₐₐ + s²ᵢ,¬ₐₐ)
```

Multi-cycle accumulation is supported by passing lists of mutant tables and data tables, enabling correlation signals to strengthen across iterative design cycles.

Sources: [Docs/Tool/Statistics.md](Docs/Tool/Statistics.md#L58-L87)

### Stage 3: BayesianAdjuster

`BayesianAdjuster` closes the loop by converting correlation signals into adjusted mutation frequencies for the next design cycle. It applies a Bayesian log-odds update:

```
p(i, aa | c) = σ(σ⁻¹(p₀(i, aa)) + γ · c(i, aa))
```

The `gamma` hyperparameter controls adjustment aggressiveness (default 3.0), while `pseudocount` (default 0.01) prevents zero-probability lock-in and allows beneficial but previously unobserved mutations to "resurrect." The `mode` parameter sets optimization direction: `"min"` for metrics where lower is better (binding affinity), `"max"` for higher-is-better (activity). Output includes both absolute and relative normalized probabilities, plus a detailed adjustment log.

```python
from biopipelines.bayesian_adjuster import BayesianAdjuster

adjuster = BayesianAdjuster(
    frequencies=profiler.tables.absolute_frequencies,
    correlations=correlation.tables.correlation_2d,
    mode="min",      # Minimize affinity
    gamma=3.0,       # Adjustment strength
    pseudocount=0.01 # Resurrection threshold
)
```

Sources: [Docs/Tool/Statistics.md](Docs/Tool/Statistics.md#L105-L130)

## Data Export and ID Management

### ExtractMetrics

`ExtractMetrics` creates separate CSV files per metric from multiple input tables, formatted for direct import into GraphPad Prism or similar statistical software. Given multiple condition tables and a list of metric column names, it produces one CSV per metric with each table's values as a separate column. The `table_names` parameter provides human-readable condition labels.

Sources: [extract_metrics.py](biopipelines/extract_metrics.py#L5-L11), [extract_metrics.py](biopipelines/extract_metrics.py#L56-L60)

### ReMap

`ReMap` renames IDs across all streams and tables of a source output, supporting auto-numbering (`"design"` → `design_1`), explicit lists, dictionary mappings, or alignment onto another tool's IDs. At execution time, files are symlinked and CSV tables are rewritten. The `map` parameter enables provenance bridging — remapping tool A's IDs onto tool C's schema while maintaining tool B as an intermediate reference.

Sources: [Docs/Tool/DataManagement.md](Docs/Tool/DataManagement.md#L67-L87)

## Typical Analysis-Filtering Workflow

The following flowchart shows a canonical workflow for analyzing and filtering Boltz2 predictions, demonstrating how structural metrics feed into Panda for multi-criteria selection:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Boltz2 predictions"] --> D["Distance<br/>(binding proximity)"]
    A --> C["Contacts<br/>(interface analysis)"]
    A --> P["PoseChange<br/>(pose validation)"]

    D --> M["Panda merge"]
    C --> M
    P --> M

    M --> F["Panda filter<br/>(multi-criteria)"]
    F --> S["Panda sort + head<br/>(select best N)"]
    S --> R["ReMap<br/>(clean IDs)"]
    R --> X["ExportMetrics<br/>(for plotting)"]
```

This pattern — compute independent metrics, merge into a unified table, apply filtering expressions, select top candidates — is the standard analysis idiom in biopipelines. Each metric tool produces a table keyed by structure ID; Panda's `merge` (with `on=None`) automatically joins on these IDs; and the `filter` expression can reference any column from any merged table. The `pool` parameter then propagates the selection back to the physical structure files.

For iterative design workflows — where analysis informs the next generation of designs — the mutation analysis pipeline (MutationProfiler → SequenceMetricCorrelation → BayesianAdjuster → MutationComposer) replaces the terminal filtering step with a frequency-adjusted input for ProteinMPNN or LigandMPNN, enabling **machine-learning-guided sequence optimization** across design cycles.

## Environment Requirements Summary

Analysis and filtering tools span multiple conda environments depending on their computational dependencies:

| Tool | Environment | Key Dependencies |
|------|-------------|-----------------|
| Distance, Angle, Panda, Selection, ReMap, ExtractMetrics | `biopipelines` | pandas, PyMOL (for geometric tools) |
| Contacts, ConformationalChange, PoseChange | `ProteinEnv` | PyMOL |
| PoseBusters | `posebusters` | posebusters (Python 3.10) |
| CABSflex | `CABSflex` | cabs, modeller (Python 2.7) |
| MutationProfiler, SequenceMetricCorrelation, BayesianAdjuster | `MutationEnv` | seaborn, matplotlib, logomaker, scipy |

Sources: [Docs/Tool/Analysis.md](Docs/Tool/Analysis.md#L1-L20), [Docs/Tool/Statistics.md](Docs/Tool/Statistics.md#L1-L30), [posebusters.py](biopipelines/posebusters.py#L53-L60)

---

**Next Steps**: To understand how these tools integrate into the execution infrastructure, see [HelpScripts Runtime Layer](18-helpscripts-runtime-layer) for the generated script patterns that power all analysis tools at runtime. For building custom analysis tools, see [Custom Tool Development Guide](21-custom-tool-development-guide) for the BaseConfig implementation contract. For advanced data flow patterns including multi-pool filtering and cross-cycle accumulation, see [Bundle and Each Input Patterns](14-bundle-and-each-input-patterns) and [Table Reference and Provenance](16-table-reference-and-provenance).

# Bundle and Each Input Patterns



When a tool receives multiple inputs from upstream tools, biopipelines must decide how to combine them. The combinatorics system — implemented in [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py) — provides two complementary wrappers, `Each` and `Bundle`, that let you control whether inputs form a **cartesian product** or a **single grouped entity**. This page explains the mechanics, ID generation rules, and practical patterns you will encounter when building multi-input pipelines.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L5-L29)

## The Problem: Multiple Inputs, Multiple Strategies

Consider two upstream tools that each produce multiple results: `ToolA` outputs proteins *prot1, prot2* and `ToolB` outputs ligands *lig1, lig2, lig3*. When you pass both into `ToolC`, the framework must resolve one fundamental question: **how many jobs should ToolC run, and what goes into each one?** The answer is determined by how you wrap the inputs. Without any wrapper, every input is treated as an independent axis of iteration — the default `Each` behavior. Wrapping an input in `Bundle` collapses all its elements into a single group that appears together in every job configuration.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L6-L13), [boltz2.py](ExamplePipelines/boltz2.py#L96-L112)

## Each: The Cartesian Product Default

`Each` marks one or more sources as independent iteration axes. When every input to a tool uses `Each` (the default for bare values), the framework generates the full cartesian product of all input sets. This is the most common combinatorics pattern and requires no explicit wrapper at all.

```python
# Explicit Each (equivalent to bare values)
boltz = Boltz2(
    proteins=Each(protein_a, protein_b),   # 2 proteins
    ligands=ligand_library                  # 3 ligands (default: Each)
)
# → 6 predictions: prot1+lig1, prot1+lig2, prot1+lig3,
#                   prot2+lig1, prot2+lig2, prot2+lig3
```

The `Each` class itself is minimal — a thin container that holds references to source objects and signals the combinatorics engine to treat each element as a separate iteration point. Its constructor requires at least one source and stores them in the `sources` attribute for later unwrapping.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L37-L48), [boltz2.py](ExamplePipelines/boltz2.py#L96-L112)

## Bundle: Grouping Elements Together

`Bundle` collapses multiple elements into a single entity. Instead of iterating over them independently, all bundled elements are combined into one configuration that appears together in every job. This is the pattern to use when a tool should process a fixed group of items as a unit — for example, a protein complex of multiple chains, or a set of cofactors that must always be present together.

```python
# Bundle all ligands together — each protein sees all ligands at once
boltz = Boltz2(
    proteins=Each(protein_a, protein_b),
    ligands=Bundle(ligand_library)
)
# → 2 predictions:
#   ProteinA with (aspirin+caffeine+ibuprofen)
#   ProteinB with (aspirin+caffeine+ibuprofen)
```

The `Bundle` class mirrors `Each` structurally — same constructor signature, same `sources` attribute — but the combinatorics engine interprets it entirely differently. Where `Each` contributes to the cartesian product, `Bundle` collapses into a static group.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L51-L62), [boltz2.py](ExamplePipelines/boltz2.py#L115-L123)

## Input Combination Patterns

The power of this system lies in mixing `Bundle` and `Each` across different inputs. The following table summarizes every meaningful combination, using 2 proteins and 3 ligands as running inputs:

| Pattern | Code Sketch | Jobs | Output IDs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All Each** (default) | `Each(protA, protB), Each(lig1, lig2, lig3)` | 6 | `prot1+lig1`, `prot1+lig2`, …, `prot2+lig3` |
| **Bundle ligands** | `Each(protA, protB), Bundle(lig1, lig2, lig3)` | 2 | `prot1+(lig1+lig2+lig3)`, `prot2+(lig1+lig2+lig3)` |
| **Bundle proteins** | `Bundle(protA, protB), Each(lig1, lig2, lig3)` | 3 | `(protA+protB)+lig1`, `(protA+protB)+lig2`, `(protA+protB)+lig3` |
| **Bundle both** | `Bundle(protA, protB), Bundle(lig1, lig2, lig3)` | 1 | `protA+protB+lig1+lig2+lig3` |

When **all axes are bundled**, the framework produces exactly one job containing every element from every input. This is the degenerate case — no iteration, just a single combined configuration.

Sources: [boltz2.py](ExamplePipelines/boltz2.py#L96-L135), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L518-L600)

## Nested Patterns: Bundle Containing Each

The most advanced combinatorics pattern nests `Each` inside `Bundle`. This creates a hybrid: a group where some members iterate while others remain static across all iterations. The canonical use case is adding a **common cofactor** to every member of a ligand library.

```python
# Each library ligand is bundled with ATP as a cofactor
atp = Ligand("ATP")
boltz = Boltz2(
    proteins=protein_a,
    ligands=Bundle(Each(ligand_library), atp)
)
# → 3 predictions:
#   proteinA + (aspirin + ATP)
#   proteinA + (caffeine + ATP)
#   proteinA + (ibuprofen + ATP)
```

The unwrapping logic in [`_unwrap_sources`](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L217-L278) processes this recursively: when it encounters a `Bundle`, it iterates over its `sources`. Any `Each` wrapper found inside is marked with `iterate: True` (its elements generate separate jobs), while bare sources inside the `Bundle` are marked `iterate: False` (they appear statically in every job). The outer mode remains `"bundle"` so the framework knows the whole group must be assembled per-iteration.

**Order matters within a `Bundle`**. In some tools (notably Boltz2), the first ligand in a bundle determines which affinity prediction is reported. Placing `Each` before the static cofactor means affinity is calculated for the library ligand in the presence of the cofactor; reversing the order swaps the affinity target.

```python
# Affinity calculated for ATP (first in bundle) in presence of each library ligand
boltz = Boltz2(
    proteins=protein_a,
    ligands=Bundle(atp, Each(ligand_library))  # ATP is first → affinity target
)
# Affinity for: ATP (presence of aspirin), ATP (presence of caffeine), ATP (presence of ibuprofen)
```

Sources: [boltz2.py](ExamplePipelines/boltz2.py#L137-L159), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L217-L278)

## ID Generation Mechanics

Output IDs are computed at **configuration time** by `predict_output_ids_with_provenance` and must match exactly what the runtime HelpScript produces. The ID naming rules follow a strict hierarchy:

1. **Single iterated axis**: output IDs are the axis IDs directly (e.g., `prot1`, `prot2`)
2. **Multiple iterated axes**: full cartesian product joined with `+` (e.g., `prot1+lig1`, `prot1+lig2`)
3. **Pure bundle axes** (no iteration): all unique IDs joined with `+` into a single ID
4. **Mixed bundle + iterated axes**: bundle prefix prepended to iterated IDs with `+` separator

The `+` separator is semantically significant — it is distinct from `_`, which is reserved for parent→child suffix relationships (e.g., a design tool producing `protein_1`, `protein_2`). This separation ensures that `id_map_utils` can correctly match multi-axis components without ambiguity.

For nested `Bundle(Each(...), static)` patterns, static IDs are joined and positioned relative to the iterated IDs based on their order within the `Bundle`. The [`_collect_static_ids_from_value`](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L448-L478) function tracks both the static ID values and whether they appear before or after the `Each` wrapper to determine the correct output ID ordering.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L518-L600), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L688-L751)

## The Tuple Convention: Stream Naming

When a tool's combinatorics axis maps to a non-default stream, you use the **tuple convention** to tell the framework which stream to extract. A named input can be:

- A **bare value**: the parameter name doubles as the stream name
- A **2-tuple** `(value, stream_name)`: explicit stream routing
- A **3-tuple** `(value, stream_name, entity_type)`: adds entity metadata (`"protein"`, `"dna"`, `"ligand"`, etc.)

```python
# Tuple convention with entity_type metadata
generate_combinatorics_config(
    "config.json",
    proteins=(lmpnn_output, "sequences", "protein"),
    ligands=(compounds_output, "compounds", "ligand")
)
```

The [`_unpack_input`](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L147-L174) function normalizes all three forms into a consistent `(actual_value, stream_name, entity_type)` triple. This mechanism lets you pass a tool's sequence output to a parameter named `proteins` while explicitly routing through the `"sequences"` stream — keeping the provenance column named `"proteins"` in the output table.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L147-L174), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L280-L327)

## Provenance Tracking

Every combinatorics operation generates **provenance metadata** — a mapping from axis aliases to the specific input IDs that contributed to each output. For a 2×3 cartesian product of proteins and ligands, the provenance dictionary contains two lists of six entries each, aligned with the output IDs:

```python
provenance = {
    "proteins": ["prot1", "prot1", "prot1", "prot2", "prot2", "prot2"],
    "ligands":  ["lig1",  "lig2",  "lig3",  "lig1",  "lig2",  "lig3"]
}
```

For bundle axes with multiple elements, the framework emits both a combined provenance entry (all IDs joined with `+`) and indexed sub-entries (`axis.1`, `axis.2`, ...) for granular lookup. This provenance flows into the output map table, enabling downstream tools and analysis steps to trace any result back to its exact input origins.

> [!TIP]
> Provenance columns are named after the **parameter alias** (the kwarg key), not the stream name. Use the tuple convention to decouple the user-facing column name from the internal stream routing when they differ.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L518-L600), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L83-L104)

## Two-Phase Architecture: Configuration and Execution

The combinatorics system operates across two distinct phases, separated by the pipeline's save-and-submit boundary.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Configuration Time
        A[Pipeline Definition] --> B[generate_combinatorics_config]
        B --> C[CombinatoricsConfig JSON]
        B --> D[predict_output_ids]
        D --> E[Provenance Map]
    end
    subgraph Execution Time
        C --> F[HelpScript reads JSON]
        F --> G[load_ids_from_sources]
        G --> H[predict_single_output_id per iteration]
        H --> I[Tool config generated per job]
    end
```

At **configuration time**, `generate_combinatorics_config` serializes the full combinatorics description into a `CombinatoricsConfig` JSON file stored alongside the tool's execution script. This file contains every axis definition — its mode, source paths, and iterate flags — plus the predicted output IDs and provenance for validation.

At **execution time**, the tool's HelpScript reads this JSON, loads actual IDs from the CSV source files via `load_ids_from_sources`, and iterates using `predict_single_output_id` to reconstruct the exact same ID that was predicted at configuration time. This two-phase design ensures that configuration-time predictions and runtime behavior always agree, even when the actual data files change between phases (e.g., when a HelpScript filters or transforms inputs before the combinatorics step).

> [!TIP]
> The `predict_single_output_id` function always uses full cartesian naming with `+` separators, regardless of axis count. This mirrors `predict_output_ids` without the single-axis shortcut, ensuring config-time and SLURM-time ID generation produce identical strings.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L280-L327), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L688-L751), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L353-L387)

## Data Flow: From Sources to AxisConfig

The complete journey from a user's Python expression to the serialized JSON consumed by HelpScripts involves three transformations:

1. **Tuple unpacking** — `_unpack_input` normalizes bare values, 2-tuples, and 3-tuples into `(value, stream_name, entity_type)`
2. **Wrapper unwrapping** — `_unwrap_sources` recursively opens `Bundle`/`Each` wrappers and extracts CSV paths from `DataStream`, `StandardizedOutput`, or `ToolOutput` objects, tagging each source with an `iterate` flag
3. **Axis assembly** — `generate_combinatorics_config` packages the unwrapped sources into `AxisConfig` dataclasses, attaches provenance, and serializes to JSON

Each source path extracted by `_extract_source_paths` points to a map table CSV. The `iterate` flag determines whether IDs from that source expand the cartesian product or remain static within each bundle iteration.

Sources: [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L147-L278), [combinatorics.py](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L175-L215)

## Quick Reference

| Expression | Meaning | Iteration |
|---|---|---|
| `proteins=source` | Each (implicit default) | Over source IDs |
| `proteins=Each(a, b)` | Each (explicit) | Over combined IDs from a and b |
| `proteins=Bundle(a, b)` | Bundle | No iteration; a and b grouped together |
| `ligands=Bundle(Each(lib), cofactor)` | Hybrid | Over library IDs; cofactor static in each group |
| `proteins=(source, "sequences", "protein")` | Tuple routing | Each over sequences stream, entity type metadata |

| Function | Phase | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `generate_combinatorics_config` | Configuration | Main entry point; builds and saves JSON config |
| `predict_output_ids_with_provenance` | Configuration | Computes output IDs and provenance mapping |
| `predict_single_output_id` | Execution | Reconstructs one output ID per iteration in HelpScripts |
| `load_ids_from_sources` | Execution | Reads actual IDs from CSV source files |
| `is_combinatorics_wrapper` | Configuration | Type check for Bundle/Each presence |

For the broader context of how these patterns fit into pipeline construction, see [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container) for the underlying data representation and [Pipeline Orchestration Engine](6-pipeline-orchestration-engine) for how tools consume combinatorics configs during script generation. The ID patterns produced by these combinations are described in detail in [Pattern-Based ID Expansion](15-pattern-based-id-expansion).

# Pattern-Based ID Expansion



BioPipelines uses a declarative pattern language to represent large ID spaces compactly. Instead of materializing every identifier at configuration time, the framework stores symbolic patterns in `DataStream` objects and expands them lazily—only when a specific count, index, or file path is needed. This design keeps pipeline configuration lightweight even when a single tool produces thousands of designs, and it enables a two-phase execution model where config-time prediction coexists with runtime certainty.

## Pattern Syntax Reference

The pattern system recognizes two delimiter styles—angle brackets for deterministic slots and square brackets for runtime-dependent (lazy) slots. The core module is [id_patterns.py](biopipelines/id_patterns.py), which is deliberately standalone with no DataStream imports.

### Deterministic Slots `<…>`

Deterministic slots are expanded fully at configuration time using the regex `_SLOT_RE = re.compile(r'<([^>\[\]]+)>')` at [line 25](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L25-L25). They support two internal grammars:

| Syntax | Expansion | Example | Result |
|--------|-----------|---------|--------|
| `<N..M>` | Inclusive numeric range | `<0..49>` | `0, 1, …, 49` (50 values) |
| `<A B C>` | Explicit space-separated set | `<A V I L>` | `A, V, I, L` (4 values) |

Multiple slots in a single string compute their **Cartesian product**, ordered by slot position. The expansion engine uses `itertools.product` and substitutes slots in reverse order to preserve positional indices [lines 184–192](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L184-L192).

```python
'<0..2>_<A B>'  →  ['0_A', '0_B', '1_A', '1_B', '2_A', '2_B']
```

A single DataStream `ids` list can contain multiple pattern strings; each is expanded independently and concatenated. For instance, `ids=["5HG6_<0..4>", "UBQ_<0..9>"]` represents 15 distinct items.

### Lazy (Runtime) Slots `[…]`

Square bracket segments mark portions of an ID that cannot be resolved until execution completes. The helper `is_lazy()` at [line 36](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L36-L38) detects them via `_BRACKET_RE = re.compile(r'\[([^\]]+)\]')` at [line 28](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L28-L28). Attempting to fully expand a lazy pattern raises `LazyPatternError` [line 31](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L31-L33).

```
prot_<0..4>[_<N><S A L K>]
├── Deterministic prefix: prot_<0..4>  →  5 IDs at config time
└── Lazy suffix: [_<N><S A L K>]       →  resolved at runtime
```

The function `try_expand()` at [line 58](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L58-L73) returns a tuple `(ids, is_complete)` where `is_complete` is `False` when brackets remain. The function `strip_brackets()` at [line 46](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L46-L55) removes all bracket segments, yielding the deterministic prefix. The function `glob_from_lazy()` at [line 76](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L76-L83) replaces brackets with `*` for filesystem globbing.

## Two-Phase Expansion Architecture

The pattern system implements a deliberate split between configuration-time prediction and runtime resolution. This is not a performance optimization alone—it is the mechanism by which the pipeline validates structure without knowing exact outputs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Tool definition<br/>(Python config-time)"] --> B{"Contains patterns?"}
    B -- Yes --> C["count_pattern() / count_ids()<br/>Predict item count"]
    B -- No --> D["Use literal IDs directly"]
    C --> E["try_expand()<br/>Expand deterministic prefix only"]
    E --> F["Pipeline validation<br/>SLURM resource estimation<br/>Dependency ordering"]
    F --> G["Tool execution<br/>(Bash runtime)"]
    G --> H["HelpScript writes map_table<br/>with fully-expanded IDs"]
    H --> I["DataStream reads map_table<br/>at runtime (_runtime_mode=True)"]
    D --> F
```

At configuration time, `len(stream)` calls `count_ids()` at [line 158](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L158-L160), which sums per-pattern counts without materializing any strings. This means a pattern like `design_<0..999>` reports `len == 1000` in O(k) where k is the number of slots, not the number of IDs.

At runtime, when `_runtime_mode` is `True` on the DataStream, the `ids_expanded` property at [lines 118–136](biopipelines/datastream.py#L118-L136) reads fully materialized IDs directly from the `map_table` CSV written by the bash HelpScript:

```python
if self._runtime_mode:
    # Runtime: fully-expanded IDs are in the map_table written by bash
    self._ids_expanded = list(self._get_map_data()['id'])
else:
    # Config time: expand only the deterministic prefix
    self._ids_expanded, _ = id_patterns.try_expand_ids(self.ids)
```

## O(1) Index Access for Single-Slot Patterns

A critical performance feature is `expand_at()` at [line 243](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L243-L277). For single-slot patterns, it computes the indexed element directly from the range parameters without generating the full list:

```python
# expand_at('design_<0..999>', 42) → 'design_42'  — O(1)
# expand_at('<0..2>_<A B>', 4)     → '1_B'         — O(k) slots, not O(n) items
```

The algorithm decomposes the flat index into per-slot indices using row-major order division. The DataStream `__getitem__` at [lines 205–250](biopipelines/datastream.py#L205-L250) exploits this for integer indexing when `len(self.ids) == 1` (single-pattern case).

> [!TIP]
> When iterating a DataStream in a notebook, `__getitem__` uses `expand_at` for O(1) random access on single-slot patterns. This means `stream[99999]` on `ids=["design_<0..99999>"]` does not allocate a 100k-element list. However, slicing or multi-pattern IDs triggers full expansion.

## File Pattern Templates

File paths use a separate template mechanism distinct from ID slots. The `<id>` placeholder in a file template is substituted per expanded ID via `expand_file_pattern()` at [line 280](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L280-L285):

```python
# DataStream with template
DataStream(
    ids=["5HG6_<0..3>"],
    files=["output/<id>.pdb"],
    format="pdb"
)
# files_expanded → ["output/5HG6_0.pdb", "output/5HG6_1.pdb", ...]
```

The `files_expanded` property at [lines 139–158](biopipelines/datastream.py#L139-L158) detects the `<id>` template when `len(files) == 1 and '<id>' in files[0]`. When lazy patterns are present, the glob variant `glob_from_lazy_ids()` at [line 86](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L86-L99) replaces bracket segments with `*` before expanding deterministic slots, producing glob-ready paths like `prot_0*+9DP.pdb`.

## Pattern Composition in Combinatorics

The [combinatorics module](biopipelines/combinatorics.py) uses pattern composition to generate downstream IDs without expanding parent patterns. The function `generate_multiplied_ids_pattern()` at [line 792](biopipelines/combinatorics.py#L792-L817) appends a suffix pattern to each parent ID string:

```python
generate_multiplied_ids_pattern(
    ["5HG6_<0..4>"], "<1..3>"
)
→ ["5HG6_<0..4>_<1..3>"]   # 5 × 3 = 15 items, zero allocations
```

This is the mechanism behind multi-step pipelines. When ProteinMPNN generates 10 sequences per input structure, the tool appends `_<1..10>` to each parent ID pattern. The resulting composed pattern propagates through the pipeline without ever expanding the intermediate lists. The helper `append_suffix()` at [line 311](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L311-L317) provides the same composition for standalone use.

The constructor helpers `make_range()` and `make_set()` at [lines 295–308](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L295-L308) offer programmatic pattern construction:

```python
make_range('design', 0, 49)          → 'design_<0..49>'
make_set('pos', ['42A', '42V', '42W']) → 'pos_<42A 42V 42W>'
```

## Deduplication and Containment

When a pipeline mixes literal IDs with patterns that already cover them, `dedup_parent_children()` at [line 222](biopipelines/id_patterns.py#L222-L240) eliminates the redundancy:

```python
dedup_parent_children(['prot_<0..2>', 'prot_0', 'prot_1'])
→ ['prot_<0..2>']
```

It expands each pattern string and removes any literal IDs found in the expanded set. For lazy patterns, it uses `try_expand()` to avoid raising `LazyPatternError`.

## Complete API Surface

| Function | Purpose | Raises on |
|----------|---------|-----------|
| `contains_pattern(s)` | Detect `<…>` slots | — |
| `is_lazy(s)` / `has_brackets(s)` | Detect `[…]` segments | — |
| `is_literal(s)` | No pattern slots at all | — |
| `count_pattern(s)` | Count expanded size without expanding | — |
| `count_ids(ids)` | Sum counts across list | — |
| `expand_pattern(s)` | Full expansion to string list | `LazyPatternError` |
| `expand_ids(ids)` | Expand each element and concatenate | `LazyPatternError` |
| `try_expand(s)` | Expand prefix, return `(ids, is_complete)` | — |
| `try_expand_ids(ids)` | Batch `try_expand` | — |
| `expand_at(s, index)` | O(1) single element by index | `IndexError` |
| `strip_brackets(s)` | Remove `[…]` segments | — |
| `glob_from_lazy(s)` | Replace `[…]` with `*` | — |
| `glob_from_lazy_ids(ids)` | Glob-ready expanded file paths | — |
| `expand_file_pattern(template, id)` | Substitute `<id>` placeholder | — |
| `file_has_glob(template)` | Check for `*` wildcard | — |
| `make_range(base, start, end)` | Build `base_<start..end>` | — |
| `make_set(base, values)` | Build `base_<v1 v2 …>` | — |
| `append_suffix(parent_ids, suffix)` | Append pattern suffix | — |
| `dedup_parent_children(ids)` | Remove literals covered by patterns | — |

## Relationship to Multi-Axis IDs

Pattern expansion operates independently from the multi-axis combinatorics system described in [Bundle and Each Input Patterns](14-bundle-and-each-input-patterns). The two systems serve different purposes: **patterns** compactly represent enumerations within a single axis (e.g., "10 designs per structure"), while **combinatorics** control how multiple input axes are combined (e.g., "3 proteins × 5 ligands"). Multi-axis IDs use `+` as separator (e.g., `prot1+lig1`), while pattern-generated suffixes use `_` (e.g., `prot1_3`). The [id_map_utils module](biopipelines/id_map_utils.py) respects this distinction when matching IDs across tables, splitting on `+` for provenance resolution while using `_<S>` or `_<N>` patterns for suffix stripping.

## Next Steps

- **[Bundle and Each Input Patterns](14-bundle-and-each-input-patterns)** — How pattern-composed IDs interact with cartesian product and bundling across multiple input axes.
- **[Table Reference and Provenance](16-table-reference-and-provenance)** — How `id_map_utils` resolves pattern-expanded IDs back to their parent sources using recursive suffix stripping.
- **[DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container)** — The full DataStream lifecycle including pattern-aware iteration, filtering, and serialization.

# Table Reference and Provenance



Tables are the connective tissue of a biopipelines workflow. Every tool that produces structured output emits one or more named tables — CSV files on disk whose schema is declared at configuration time. Downstream tools consume these tables by name, reference individual columns by attribute access, and automatically inherit the provenance chain that links every output row back to its input origins. This page documents the table lifecycle from creation through column reference, transformation, and provenance tracking.

## Table Architecture Overview

The table subsystem spans four architectural layers: tool output declaration, configuration-time metadata, runtime CSV materialization, and downstream reference resolution. At the center sits `TableInfo`, a dual-purpose object that both describes a table's schema and acts as a factory for column references consumed by subsequent tools.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Tool Output Declaration"
        A[BaseConfig.get_output_files] -->|"returns TableInfo"| B[TableInfo]
    end

    subgraph "Metadata & Reference Layer"
        B -->|" delegates to"| C[TableMetadata]
        B -->|" attribute access"| D["TableReference(path, column)"]
        B -->|" dot access"| E["TableInfo.score → TableReference"]
    end

    subgraph "Container Layer"
        F[TableContainer] -->|" tables.designs"| B
        G[IndexedTableContainer] -->|" indexed by ID"| B
        H["ToolOutput.tables"] -->|" delegates to"| F
        I["StandardizedOutput"] -->|" .tables"| F
        J["StreamContainer"] -->|" .streams"| K["DataStream"]
    end

    subgraph "External Table Source"
        L[Table entity] -->|" reads CSV/Excel"| B
    end

    subgraph "Provenance (Map Table)"
        K -->|" map_table CSV"| M["{stream}.id columns"]
        M -->|" get_id_provenance"| N["{output_id → parent_id}"]
    end

    subgraph "Consumer Tools"
        D -->|" serialized to pipe script"| O[Panda / downstream tool]
        P[table_utils] -->|" runtime access"| B
    end
```

## TableInfo: Schema Description and Column Factory

`TableInfo` is the central abstraction that every tool returns when it declares tabular output. It wraps a `TableMetadata` object holding the table's name, filesystem path, column list, description, and row count. More importantly, `TableInfo` intercepts any attribute access that does not match its own properties and returns a `TableReference` — a lightweight serializable tuple of `(path, column_name)` that downstream tools can resolve at runtime.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L753-L801)

The `TableMetadata` dataclass holds the raw schema fields and is exposed through the `.info` property. This separation ensures that metadata access never accidentally creates a column reference — only the explicit `.info` prefix reaches the metadata layer, while every other attribute name is assumed to be a column.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L738-L774)

```python
# TableInfo declared by ProteinMPNN
tables = {
    "sequences": TableInfo(
        name="sequences",
        path="/output/pipeline/ProteinMPNN/queries.csv",
        columns=["id", "structures.id", "source_pdb", "sequence", "score", "seq_recovery", "gaps"],
        description="ProteinMPNN sequence results",
        count=100
    )
}

# Metadata access
tables["sequences"].info.path       # "/output/pipeline/ProteinMPNN/queries.csv"
tables["sequences"].info.columns    # ["id", "structures.id", ...]
tables["sequences"].info.count      # 100

# Column reference (any attribute becomes TableReference)
tables["sequences"].score           # TableReference(path, "score")
tables["sequences"].seq_recovery    # TableReference(path, "seq_recovery")
```

## TableContainer and IndexedTableContainer

When a tool's `get_output_files()` returns a `tables` dictionary, the pipeline wraps it in a `TableContainer` at configuration time. `TableContainer` supports both dictionary-style access (`tables["sequences"]`) and attribute access (`tables.sequences`), returning `TableInfo` objects in either case. This is the object you interact with through `ToolOutput.tables`.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L924-L1000)

Some tools produce one table per input ID — for example, a per-residue RMSF calculation yields a separate CSV for each structure. These tools return an `IndexedTableContainer` instead of a plain `TableInfo`. An `IndexedTableContainer` maps entry IDs to individual `TableInfo` objects, all sharing a common schema, and integrates into `TableContainer` as a single named entry. You retrieve individual tables by ID using bracket notation.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L804-L920)

| Container | Use Case | Access Pattern | Result |
|-----------|----------|----------------|--------|
| `TableInfo` | Single output table | `tables.sequences` | `TableInfo` with `.info` and column references |
| `IndexedTableContainer` | One table per input ID | `tables.rmsf["1a2j"]` | `TableInfo` for that specific ID |
| `TableContainer` | Named collection | `tables.keys()` | All table names in the output |

## The Table Entity: Loading External Data

The `Table` class extends `BaseConfig` to provide a zero-execution entity that loads an existing CSV or Excel file into the pipeline at configuration time. It reads column headers and row counts immediately, then wraps the file in a `TableInfo` that downstream tools can reference exactly as if the table had been produced by a computational tool. Excel files are transparently converted to CSV on first load.

Sources: [table.py](biopipelines/table.py#L26-L164)

This is particularly useful for injecting pre-computed metrics, experimental data, or external design specifications into a pipeline without any runtime computation. The `Table` entity generates a no-op bash script — its output already exists on disk.

Sources: [table.py](biopipelines/table.py#L123-L137)

```python
# Load an external table
metrics = Table("/path/to/experimental_metrics.csv", name="experimental")

# Reference its columns in downstream tools — identical to tool-produced tables
mpnn = ProteinMPNN(
    structures=proteins,
    fixed=(metrics.tables.experimental, "fixed_residues")
)
```

## Column References: The TableReference Protocol

The `TableReference` mechanism is what enables tools to accept "a specific column from a specific table" as a parameter. When you write `mpnn_fixed = af_output.tables.structures.fixed`, the attribute access on `TableInfo` returns a `TableReference` containing the table's CSV path and the column name `"fixed"`. At script generation time, the tool serializes this reference into the bash script, and the corresponding HelpScript reads the column values at runtime.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L776-L782)

ProteinMPNN exemplifies this pattern: its `fixed` and `redesigned` parameters accept either a PyMOL-style selection string or a `(TableInfo, column_name)` tuple. When a `TableReference` is provided, the HelpScript `pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py` reads per-structure fixed-position specifications from the referenced CSV column rather than applying a uniform selection to all inputs.

Sources: [protein_mpnn.py](biopipelines/protein_mpnn.py#L115-L172)

## Table Utilities: Runtime Navigation

The `table_utils` module provides a small set of functions for accessing tables at runtime from any output source format. These functions handle the polymorphism between `ToolOutput`, `StandardizedOutput`, and raw dictionaries, giving HelpScripts a uniform access layer.

Sources: [table_utils.py](biopipelines/table_utils.py#L1-L133)

| Function | Purpose | Returns |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `get_table(source, name)` | Retrieve `TableInfo` by name | `TableInfo` or raises `KeyError` |
| `get_table_path(source, name)` | Get the CSV filesystem path | `str` path |
| `list_tables(source)` | List all available table names | `List[str]` |
| `get_indexed_table(source, name, entry_id)` | Get a per-ID table from an `IndexedTableContainer` | `TableInfo` |
| `table_exists(source, name)` | Check if a named table is available | `bool` |

> [!TIP]
> `get_table` resolves through multiple source types in order: raw dictionary → object with `.tables` attribute (including `ToolOutput` and `StandardizedOutput`). This means HelpScripts can accept outputs from any tool without type-checking, since all tools conform to the same `get_output_files()` contract.

## Map Tables and Provenance Columns

Every `DataStream` may carry a `map_table` — a CSV file that minimally contains `id`, `file`, and `value` columns, plus any number of **provenance columns**. Provenance columns follow the naming convention `{stream_name}.id` and record which input ID produced each output ID. When ProteinMPNN generates 10 sequences per structure, the sequences map table contains a `structures.id` column that maps each sequence ID back to its parent structure ID.

Sources: [datastream.py](biopipelines/datastream.py#L430-L562)

The `create_map_table` factory function handles provenance population through two mechanisms: explicit provenance dictionaries and automatic provenance generation from `parent_ids` combined with a `suffix_pattern`. When a tool uses `suffix_pattern` (e.g., `"<1..10>"`) along with `parent_ids` and `input_stream_name`, the factory automatically replicates each parent ID once per suffix value, establishing the complete parent→child mapping without manual provenance construction.

Sources: [datastream.py](biopipelines/datastream.py#L436-L530)

```csv
# Example map table produced by ProteinMPNN (queries.csv)
id,structures.id,source_pdb,sequence,score,seq_recovery,gaps
5HG6_1,5HG6,5HG6.pdb,MTYKL...,0.82,0.91,0
5HG6_2,5HG6,5HG6.pdb,VTYKL...,0.78,0.85,0
6MRR_1,6MRR,6MRR.pdb,GLAEN...,0.85,0.93,1
6MRR_2,6MRR,6MRR.pdb,ALAEQ...,0.79,0.87,0
```

## Provenance Extraction: get_id_provenance

The `BaseConfig.get_id_provenance()` method reads every output stream's map table and extracts all `{stream_name}.id` columns into a structured mapping: `{axis_name → {output_id → parent_id}}`. This is the mechanism that enables the pipeline to trace any output back through the full chain of tools that produced it. The method deduplicates by tracking which map tables it has already visited, avoiding redundant reads when multiple streams share the same underlying CSV.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L374-L423)

```python
# Called on any tool config — returns all provenance from its output streams
provenance = mpnn_config.get_id_provenance()
# {
#     "structures": {
#         "5HG6_1": "5HG6",
#         "5HG6_2": "5HG6",
#         "6MRR_1": "6MRR",
#         "6MRR_2": "6MRR"
#     }
# }
```

This provenance data is particularly critical when tools produce N outputs per input (as with `num_sequences` in ProteinMPNN or `num_designs` in RFdiffusion). Without the provenance column, there would be no way to associate a generated sequence like `5HG6_2` back to its originating structure `5HG6`.

## Table Transformation with Panda

The `Panda` tool consumes `TableInfo` objects (or `StandardizedOutput` wrappers) and applies a chain of pandas-style operations — filtering, sorting, merging, concatenation, calculated columns, and more. Panda accepts tables as positional arguments or via the `tables` parameter, and operations as a list of `Operation` objects created through `Panda`'s static methods.

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L53-L1005)

```python
# Sort ProteinMPNN outputs by score, take top 50, merge with experimental data
Panda(
    tables=[mpnn_output.tables.sequences, metrics.tables.experimental],
    operations=[
        Panda.sort("score", ascending=False),
        Panda.head(50),
        Panda.merge(on="id", how="inner")
    ]
)
```

Each `Operation` is a `dataclass` with a `type` string and a `params` dictionary, serialized to JSON for the runtime HelpScript. Panda also produces its own output table, which becomes a `TableInfo` consumable by subsequent tools — maintaining the same reference chain through the pipeline.

Sources: [panda.py](biopipelines/panda.py#L30-L50)

## Missing Table Propagation

Tools that filter or deduplicate output emit a `missing` table recording which IDs were removed and why. The `missing` table carries columns `id`, `removed_by` (the tool name), and `cause` (the reason for removal). When a downstream tool needs to propagate this information, it calls `BaseConfig._get_upstream_missing_table_path()` to locate any `missing` table from its inputs and passes the path to its HelpScript via an `--upstream-missing` flag.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L658-L690)

This mechanism ensures that if ProteinMPNN removes duplicate sequences, and those sequences are then passed to AlphaFold, AlphaFold's missing table will include both its own removals and the upstream ProteinMPNN removals — providing a complete audit trail.

## Serialization and Runtime Resolution

`TableInfo` objects serialize to plain dictionaries via `to_dict()`, containing `name`, `path`, `columns`, `description`, and `count`. `IndexedTableContainer` extends this with a `_type` discriminator and an `entries` mapping. The pipeline persists these dictionaries in tool configuration JSON, and the runtime HelpScript layer reads them back. The `TableReference` objects themselves are not serialized directly — instead, the tool's `generate_script()` method renders the `(path, column)` pair into the bash script as string arguments that the HelpScript interprets.

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L793-L801), [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L882-L911)

The `DataStreamResolver` provides the inverse operation: converting any input format (file paths, dictionaries, existing DataStreams) into a `DataStream` with an auto-generated map table. This resolver is used by tools that need to construct streams from heterogeneous inputs, ensuring that every stream — regardless of origin — carries the same map table structure for provenance and runtime lookup.

Sources: [datastream_resolver.py](biopipelines/datastream_resolver.py#L18-L163)

---

For the pipeline mechanism that produces `ToolOutput` and `StandardizedOutput` wrapping these tables, see [Pipeline Orchestration Engine](6-pipeline-orchestration-engine). For the `DataStream` container that holds map tables and drives pattern-based ID expansion, see [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container). For the pattern system used in provenance suffix generation, see [Pattern-Based ID Expansion](15-pattern-based-id-expansion).

# SLURM Cluster Integration



BioPipelines bridges the gap between declarative pipeline definition and HPC execution by generating SLURM job scripts, managing multi-batch job chaining, and providing a unified submission interface. This page covers the complete lifecycle—from how the `Pipeline` class produces SLURM scripts, through the shell scripts that submit and monitor them, to the configuration that ties your cluster environment to the framework.

## Execution Architecture Overview

The SLURM integration operates as a two-stage pipeline: Python-based script generation followed by bash-based submission and execution. The `Pipeline` class generates all necessary SLURM wrapper scripts and pipeline execution scripts during the **save phase**, then the `submit` shell script orchestrates their submission to the cluster.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Python Pipeline Script\n(.py / .ipynb)"] -->|execute| B["Pipeline.save()\ngenerates scripts"]
    B --> C["RunTime/slurm.sh\nor slurm_batch*.sh"]
    B --> D["RunTime/pipeline.sh\nor pipeline_batch*.sh"]
    B --> E["RunTime/NNN_ToolName.sh\n(per-tool scripts)"]
    
    C -->|submitted by| F["submit script\n(bash)"]
    F -->|sbatch| G["SLURM Scheduler"]
    G -->|allocates resources| H["Compute Node"]
    H -->|executes| D
    D -->|calls| E
    E -->|activates envs| I["Tool Execution\nconda/mamba activate"]
    I -->|results| J["Output & Logs"]
    
    K["config.yaml\ncluster section"] -->|"env_manager,\nslurm_modules, emails"| F
    K -->|"module_load_line,\ncontainer_executor"| C
```

The key architectural insight is that **pipeline definition and cluster submission are decoupled**: the Python layer never calls `sbatch` directly. Instead, it generates SLURM-compatible shell scripts that the `submit` bash wrapper feeds to the scheduler. This separation allows the same pipeline definition to be executed locally via the `run` script or on any SLURM cluster via `submit`.

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L42-L120), [submit](submit#L1-L50), [config.yaml](config.yaml#L130-L153)

## Cluster Configuration

All cluster-specific settings live under the `cluster` key in `config.yaml`. The `ConfigManager` singleton reads these values and injects them into generated SLURM scripts and submission workflows.

| Setting | Type | Purpose | Default |
|---------|------|---------|---------|
| `env_manager` | `string` | Shell environment manager: `"mamba"` or `"conda"` | `"mamba"` |
| `container_executor` | `string` | Container runtime for wrapped tools: `"apptainer"` or `"singularity"` | `"apptainer"` |
| `slurm_modules` | `list[string]` | Modules to `module load` at the top of every SLURM script | `["miniforge3", "apptainer"]` |
| `emails` | `map<string, string>` | Unix username → notification email (used with `email="auto"`) | `{}` |

The `ConfigManager` consumes these through targeted accessors. The shell hook command is derived from `env_manager`—for mamba it generates `eval "$(mamba shell hook --shell bash)"`, and the module load line is assembled from `slurm_modules` as `module load miniforge3 apptainer`. Both are embedded directly into generated SLURM wrapper scripts.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L130-L153), [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L144-L211)

## Resource Specification and Batch Boundaries

The `Resources()` method (and its instance-level counterpart `pipeline.resources()`) is the primary mechanism for declaring computational requirements. Each call to `Resources()` creates a **new batch boundary**—tools added after one `Resources()` call and before the next belong to that batch and share its resource allocation.

### GPU Specification Grammar

The GPU parameter supports a rich specification language that maps to SLURM constraint directives:

| Spec | Generated SBATCH | Behavior |
|------|-------------------|----------|
| `"A100"`, `"H100"`, `"V100"`, `"L4"` | `--gpus=1` | Request exactly 1 GPU of named model |
| `"gpu"` or `"any"` | `--gpus=1` | Any available GPU |
| `"24GB"`, `"32GB"`, `"80GB"`, `"96GB"` | `--gpus=1 --constraint="GPUMEM32GB"` | Memory-based GPU selection |
| `"32GB\|80GB\|96GB"` | `--gpus=1 --constraint="GPUMEM32GB\|GPUMEM80GB\|GPUMEM96GB"` | Accept multiple memory tiers |
| `"high-memory"` | `--gpus=1 --constraint="GPUMEM32GB\|GPUMEM80GB\|GPUMEM96GB"` | Shorthand for 32+ GB |
| `"!L4"` | `--gpus=1 --constraint="GPUMEM32GB\|GPUMEM80GB\|GPUMEM96GB"` | Exclude L4 (maps to high-memory) |
| `"!T4"` | `--gpus=1 --constraint="~GPUT4"` | Exclude T4 (generic exclusion) |
| `None` or `"none"` | *(no GPU line)* | CPU-only batch |

When a GPU is requested, the generated SLURM script also includes a diagnostic line that prints the allocated GPU model via `nvidia-smi` at job start, providing immediate visibility into resource allocation.

### Resource Inheritance

Subsequent `Resources()` calls inherit unspecified values from the previous batch. The first batch defaults to `memory="15GB"` and `time="24:00:00"` if left unspecified. Additional SLURM parameters (like `cpus`, `nodes`, `partition`) can be passed as keyword arguments and are translated to SBATCH directives with automatic underscore-to-hyphen conversion (e.g., `cpus=32` becomes `--cpus-per-task=32`).

> [!TIP]
> **Batch boundaries are implicit.** Every `Resources()` call creates a new batch. If you need five tools to share one GPU allocation and three to run CPU-only, place exactly two `Resources()` calls in your pipeline—tools are assigned to batches in the order they are added.

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L913-L985), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L660-L683)

## SLURM Script Generation

The `Pipeline.slurm()` method triggers script generation. If the pipeline has not yet been saved (via `save()` or `Save()`), it calls `save()` automatically before generating SLURM wrappers.

### Single-Batch Pipelines

When only one `Resources()` call exists, a single `slurm.sh` is generated in the `RunTime/` directory. The script contains all SBATCH directives, the module load line from config, a GPU diagnostic block (if applicable), and the full pipeline execution script inline.

The generated script includes `umask 002` to ensure all output files are group-writable—a practical choice for shared HPC environments where collaborators need access to each other's results.

### Multi-Batch Pipelines

Multiple `Resources()` calls produce a set of files:

- **`slurm_batch1.sh`, `slurm_batch2.sh`, ...** — One SLURM wrapper per batch
- **`pipeline_batch1.sh`, `pipeline_batch2.sh`, ...** — One pipeline execution script per batch
- **`config_batch1.sh`, `config_batch2.sh`, ...** — Configuration display scripts per batch

Each batch SLURM script (batch 2+) includes a `--dependency=afterok:<JOBID>` placeholder. The `submit` script performs runtime substitution—replacing `<JOBID>` with the actual job ID returned by `sbatch --parsable` from the previous batch—creating a proper SLURM dependency chain without requiring manual intervention.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B1["slurm_batch1.sh\nno dependency"] -->|sbatch → Job 12345| SB1["Submit"]
    B2["slurm_batch2.sh\ndependency=afterok:⟨JOBID⟩"] -->|⟨JOBID⟩ → 12345\nsbatch → Job 12346| SB2["Submit"]
    B3["slurm_batch3.sh\ndependency=afterok:⟨JOBID⟩"] -->|⟨JOBID⟩ → 12346\nsbatch → Job 12347| SB3["Submit"]
    
    SB1 --> B2
    SB2 --> B3
```

### Email Notification

The `email` parameter to `slurm()` supports three modes:
- **`"auto"`** (default): Looks up the current Unix username in `cluster.emails` from `config.yaml`. Warns and disables notifications if no mapping exists.
- **`""`**: No email notifications at all.
- **Specific address**: Uses the provided email directly, generating `--mail-type=END,FAIL` and `--mail-user=` directives.

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L610-L829), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L714-L756)

## External Job Dependencies

The `Dependencies()` convenience function (or `pipeline.set_dependencies()`) lets a pipeline wait for unrelated SLURM jobs to complete before its first batch starts. The dependency is injected as `--dependency=afterok:JOBID1:JOBID2` into the first batch's SLURM script, while subsequent batches retain their internal chaining logic.

```python
with Pipeline("DrugScreen", "V2", "Compound screening with dependencies"):
    Dependencies("88432150")              # Wait for external job
    Resources(gpu="A100", memory="32GB", time="24:00:00")
    tool1 = Boltz2(...)
```

This pattern enables orchestrating multi-pipeline workflows where one pipeline's output feeds another—chain them with `Dependencies()` using the job ID printed by `submit`.

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L898-L912), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1507-L1541)

## The `submit` Script

The `submit` bash script at the repository root is the primary entry point for cluster execution. It handles environment initialization, pipeline generation, output parsing, and SLURM submission in a single command.

### Execution Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["./submit pipeline.py"] --> PARSE["Parse CLI args\n(-v for verbose)"]
    PARSE --> READ_CFG["Read config.yaml\nenv_manager, slurm_modules"]
    READ_CFG --> MOD_LOAD["module load\n(slurm_modules from config)"]
    MOD_LOAD --> HOOK["Initialize shell hook\n(mamba/conda)"]
    HOOK --> ACTIVATE["Activate biopipelines env"]
    ACTIVATE --> EXEC["python pipeline.py\n(capture stdout/stderr)"]
    EXEC -->|exit ≠ 0| ERR["Print errors\nsuggest -v"]
    EXEC -->|exit = 0| PARSE_OUT["Parse output for\n*/RunTime paths"]
    PARSE_OUT -->|no paths found| FALLBACK["Look for sbatch commands\n(backward compat)"]
    PARSE_OUT -->|paths found| DETECT{"Multi-batch?\nslurm_batch*.sh exists?"}
    DETECT -->|Yes| MULTI["Chain submit with\n⟨JOBID⟩ replacement"]
    DETECT -->|No| SINGLE["Submit slurm.sh\ndirectly"]
```

The script performs several important behaviors:
- **Environment bootstrapping**: Reads `env_manager` from `config.yaml` via grep (avoiding a Python dependency at this stage) and initializes the appropriate shell hook before running the pipeline script.
- **Module loading**: Loads all modules listed in `cluster.slurm_modules` before pipeline execution.
- **Output parsing**: Scans pipeline stdout for `RunTime` directory paths using a grep pattern (`/[^ ]*/RunTime`), then looks for SLURM scripts within those directories.
- **Error filtering**: In non-verbose mode, still surfaces full tracebacks and lines matching `*Error:` or `*Exception:` patterns so failures are diagnosable without re-running.
- **Batch chaining**: For multi-batch pipelines, iterates through `slurm_batch*.sh` files in sorted order, substitutes the `<JOBID>` placeholder with the previous submission's actual job ID, and submits sequentially.

Sources: [submit](submit#L16-L57), [submit](submit#L81-L260), [submit](submit#L265-L311)

## The `resubmit` Script

The `resubmit` script handles the common case of re-running a failed or modified SLURM job without overwriting previous output. Given a path to any `slurm.sh` file, it:
