1. Extracts the job name from the `#SBATCH --job-name=` directive (falls back to the parent folder name)
2. Finds the next available `slurm_N.out` number in the script's directory
3. Submits via `sbatch` with the original script but a new output file

This ensures incremental output preservation—each resubmission gets its own log file (`slurm_1.out`, `slurm_2.out`, ...).

Sources: [resubmit](resubmit#L1-L55)

## Local Execution: The `run` Script

The `run` script mirrors `submit`'s interface but executes pipelines locally instead of submitting to SLURM. It shares the same environment initialization logic (config reading, module loading, conda activation) and the same output parsing approach, but executes `pipeline.sh` or `pipeline_batch*.sh` directly via `bash` instead of `sbatch`. Multi-batch pipelines execute sequentially in the local shell.

This is the natural counterpart for development and debugging—iterate locally with `./run pipeline.py`, then submit to the cluster with `./submit pipeline.py` when ready.

Sources: [run](run#L1-L58), [run](run#L82-L200)

## Auto-Submission via Context Manager

When using the `with Pipeline(...)` pattern in script mode (not a notebook), the context manager's `__exit__` method automatically calls `self.slurm()` if no exception occurred and `Save()` was not explicitly called. This means a standard pipeline script generates and prints SLURM scripts upon exiting the `with` block, ready for `./submit` to pick up.

In contrast, notebook mode (`on_the_fly=True`, auto-detected for `.ipynb` files) keeps the pipeline context alive across cells and does not auto-submit—tools execute immediately via the [Two-Phase Execution Model](9-two-phase-execution-model).

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L163-L191), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1479-L1504)

## Generated Directory Structure

A typical multi-batch pipeline produces the following layout under the output folder:

```
<ProjectName>/<JobName>_001/
├── RunTime/
│   ├── slurm_batch1.sh          # SLURM wrapper for batch 1
│   ├── slurm_batch2.sh          # SLURM wrapper for batch 2 (depends on batch 1)
│   ├── pipeline_batch1.sh       # Execution script for batch 1
│   ├── pipeline_batch2.sh       # Execution script for batch 2
│   ├── config_batch1.sh         # Configuration display for batch 1
│   ├── config_batch2.sh         # Configuration display for batch 2
│   ├── 001_RFdiffusion.sh       # Per-tool script (batch 1)
│   ├── 002_ProteinMPNN.sh       # Per-tool script (batch 1)
│   ├── 003_AlphaFold.sh         # Per-tool script (batch 2)
│   ├── pipeline.py              # Copy of original pipeline script
│   ├── tool_outputs/            # Exported output metadata (JSON)
│   └── id_lineage.csv           # ID provenance tracking
├── Logs/
│   ├── 001_RFdiffusion.log
│   ├── 002_ProteinMPNN.log
│   └── 003_AlphaFold.log
├── 001_RFdiffusion/             # Tool output folder
├── 002_ProteinMPNN/
├── 003_AlphaFold/
├── job_batch1.out               # SLURM stdout (after submission)
├── job_batch2.out
└── <ProjectName>_config.txt     # Combined configuration log
```

The `FolderManager` creates the `RunTime/` and `Logs/` directories during pipeline initialization, and the output folder receives a unique numeric suffix (e.g., `_001`) to prevent collisions between runs of the same project/job combination.

Sources: [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L149-L180), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L830-L896)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Resolution |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| `env_manager not found in config.yaml` | Missing `cluster` section | Add `cluster:` with `env_manager: mamba` to `config.yaml` |
| `biopipelines environment not found` | Conda env not installed | Run `mamba env create -f Environments/biopipelines.yaml && pip install -e .` |
| `Resources() must be called before generating SLURM scripts` | No `Resources()` in pipeline | Add `Resources(...)` before any tool in the `with` block |
| `No email mapping found for user 'X'` | Username not in `cluster.emails` | Add your username and email to `config.yaml` under `cluster.emails` |
| `No runtime directories found in pipeline output` | Pipeline didn't reach save/exit | Check for errors in pipeline script, re-run with `./submit -v` |
| `<JOBID>` placeholder not replaced | Manual batch submission | Use `./submit` instead of manual `sbatch` for multi-batch pipelines |

## Summary

| Component | File | Role |
|-----------|------|------|
| Resource declaration | [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L913-L985) | `Resources()` creates batch boundaries with GPU, memory, time specs |
| SLURM script generation | [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L610-L829) | Produces `slurm.sh` or `slurm_batch*.sh` with SBATCH directives |
| Cluster config | [config.yaml](config.yaml#L130-L153) | `cluster` section: env_manager, modules, emails, container executor |
| Config accessors | [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L144-L211) | `get_env_manager()`, `get_module_load_line()`, `get_emails()` |
| Submission script | [submit](submit#L1-L311) | Environment init → pipeline execution → SLURM submission |
| Local execution | [run](run#L1-L252) | Same flow as `submit`, but executes locally via `bash` |
| Job resubmission | [resubmit](resubmit#L1-L55) | Re-submit with incremental output file naming |
| External dependencies | [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1507-L1541) | `Dependencies()` adds `afterok:` to first batch |
| Auto-submit on exit | [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L163-L191) | Context manager calls `slurm()` unless `Save()` was called |

For details on how the `Pipeline` class orchestrates tool execution before SLURM generation, see [Pipeline Orchestration Engine](6-pipeline-orchestration-engine). For the on-the-fly execution path used in notebooks (which bypasses SLURM entirely), see [Two-Phase Execution Model](9-two-phase-execution-model). For how tool environments are activated within generated scripts, see [BaseConfig: Tool Abstraction Layer](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer).

# HelpScripts Runtime Layer



The HelpScripts directory constitutes biopipelines' **runtime execution substrate** — a collection of standalone CLI scripts that bridge the gap between the framework's Python-based configuration phase and its bash-script execution phase. When a pipeline tool's `generate_script()` method emits a bash script, the actual computational work is delegated to these HelpScripts, which are invoked as subprocesses with file-path arguments rather than in-memory Python objects. This separation ensures that every pipeline step, whether executed interactively in a notebook or on a SLURM cluster, runs through a uniform, reproducible runtime interface.

Sources: [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L37-L198), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L347-L408)

## Architectural Position

HelpScripts occupy a distinct layer between the framework core and the external tools. During configuration time, `BaseConfig` subclasses define parameters, resolve dependencies, and predict outputs entirely within Python. At execution time, the generated bash script replaces all of that in-memory state with **file paths and CLI arguments**, executing HelpScripts as isolated processes. The `FolderManager` injects the `HelpScripts` folder path into every pipeline's folder dictionary, which tool configs then reference via `self.folders["HelpScripts"]` to construct absolute paths to their associated scripts.

Sources: [boltz2.py](biopipelines/boltz2.py#L101-L103), [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L182-L189)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Configuration Phase (Python)"
        A[Pipeline.__init__] --> B[FolderManager.get_folders]
        B --> C["folders['HelpScripts'] = /path/to/HelpScripts"]
        D[BaseConfig.generate_script] --> E["Bash script with<br/>$HELPSRIPTS/pipe_*.py calls"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Execution Phase (Bash → Python)"
        E -->|"subprocess.Popen"| F["pipe_boltz_config_unified.py<br/>pipe_boltz_results.py<br/>pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py<br/>..."]
        F --> G[Standalone Python scripts<br/>receive file paths as args]
        G --> H[Import from biopipelines package<br/>via sys.path manipulation]
    end
    
    subgraph "Resolution Scripts"
        I["resolve_stream_ids.py"] -.->|"expand lazy IDs"| F
        J["resolve_table_column.py"] -.->|"lookup TABLE_REFERENCE"| F
        K["resolve_stream_item.sh"] -.->|"resolve file path"| F
        L["resolve_lmpnn_positions.py"] -.->|"per-ID position lookup"| F
    end
```

## Script Taxonomy

The 60+ scripts in `HelpScripts/` fall into three functional categories, each serving a different role in the runtime lifecycle.

### Pipeline Stage Scripts (`pipe_*.py`)

These are the primary workhorses — computationally intensive Python scripts that implement the core logic for individual pipeline stages. Each is a standalone argparse-based CLI program that receives absolute file paths, processes data, and writes output files to designated locations. They are **generated** by tool configs but **executed** as independent processes, meaning they must reconstruct any needed context from the filesystem alone.

| Script | Purpose | Key Imports from biopipelines |
|--------|---------|------------------------------|
| `pipe_boltz_config_unified.py` | Generates Boltz2 YAML configs for all combinatorics input combinations | `combinatorics.predict_single_output_id`, `CombinatoricsConfig` |
| `pipe_boltz_results.py` | Rearranges Boltz2 outputs, ranks models, generates PyMOL sessions | pandas, json, csv (standalone) |
| `pipe_boltz_postprocessing.py` | Extracts confidence metrics, affinity scores, and sequences from predictions | — |
| `pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py` | Establishes fixed/designed residue selections for ProteinMPNN from structures | `pdb_parser`, `biopipelines_io`, `sele_utils` |
| `pipe_alphafold_msas.py` | Creates MSA CSV table from AlphaFold `.a3m` output files | pandas (standalone) |
| `pipe_compound_library.py` | Handles SMILES library generation, validation, deduplication, and filtering | rdkit (optional) |
| `pipe_boltzgen.py` | BoltzGen postprocessing: structure collection, sequence extraction, table conversion | Bio.PDB (optional) |
| `pipe_gnina.py` | Molecular docking result processing and scoring | — |
| `pipe_filter_execution.py` | Executes filtering logic based on metric thresholds | — |
| `pipe_mutation_composer.py` | Composes mutation variants from combinatorial specifications | — |

Sources: [pipe_boltz_config_unified.py](HelpScripts/pipe_boltz_config_unified.py#L1-L46), [pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py](HelpScripts/pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py#L10-L36), [pipe_alphafold_msas.py](HelpScripts/pipe_alphafold_msas.py#L1-L79), [pipe_compound_library.py](HelpScripts/pipe_compound_library.py#L1-L50)

### Resolution Scripts (`resolve_*.py` / `resolve_*.sh`)

These are lightweight lookup utilities that resolve references at runtime — expanding lazy ID patterns, looking up table column values, and retrieving per-item data from DataStream JSON files. They are designed to be **sourced or called inline** within bash scripts, typically via command substitution (`$(python resolve_... args)`).

| Script | Input | Output | Pattern |
|--------|-------|--------|---------|
| `resolve_stream_ids.py` | DataStream JSON path | Expanded IDs (one per line, stdout) | Handles lazy patterns via runtime mode |
| `resolve_stream_item.sh` | DataStream JSON + item_id | Resolved file path (stdout) | Bash function sourced inline |
| `resolve_table_column.py` | `TABLE_REFERENCE:path:column` + item_id | Cell value (stdout) | Delegates to `biopipelines_io` |
| `resolve_lmpnn_positions.py` | Positions JSON + struct_id | Two lines: fixed_option, redesigned_option | Minimal JSON lookup |
| `resolve_stream_ids.py` uses `load_datastream` in runtime mode, which triggers lazy ID expansion against the `map_table` — the same mechanism used during configuration-time provenance tracking but deferred to the point of actual execution. |

Sources: [resolve_stream_ids.py](HelpScripts/resolve_stream_ids.py#L1-L23), [resolve_stream_item.sh](HelpScripts/resolve_stream_item.sh#L1-L27), [resolve_table_column.py](HelpScripts/resolve_table_column.py#L1-L32), [resolve_lmpnn_positions.py](HelpScripts/resolve_lmpnn_positions.py#L1-L24)

### Service Scripts (`.sh`)

Long-running or daemon-style shell scripts that provide shared infrastructure services. The MMseqs2 client/server pair implements a job-queue architecture for distributed MSA generation across compute nodes.

| Script | Role | Execution Context |
|--------|------|-------------------|
| `mmseqs2_server_gpu.sh` | MSA generation server with GPU-accelerated MMseqs2 search | SLURM job (persistent) |
| `mmseqs2_client.sh` | Client that submits sequences and polls for results | Inline in pipeline bash script |

The MMseqs2 server script uses a `require_folder()` pattern that resolves folder paths via environment variables first, then falls back to `biopipelines-config folder <key>` — providing a two-tier resolution strategy that works both in interactive and SLURM contexts.

Sources: [mmseqs2_server_gpu.sh](HelpScripts/mmseqs2_server_gpu.sh#L22-L49), [mmseqs2_client.sh](HelpScripts/mmseqs2_client.sh#L12-C44)

## Runtime Invocation Mechanism

The complete lifecycle of a HelpScript execution follows a precise sequence. When a tool is registered with a pipeline, `Pipeline._auto_register()` configures its inputs and creates a step-numbered output folder ([pipeline.py#L308-L323](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L308-L323)). During `save()` or on-the-fly execution, `BaseConfig.generate_script()` produces a bash script that references HelpScripts via the `HELPSCRIPTS` variable (injected by the pipeline script generator). The resulting bash script contains lines like:

```bash
HELPSCRIPTS="/absolute/path/to/HelpScripts"
python "$HELPSCRIPTS/pipe_boltz_config_unified.py" \
    "/runtime/001_Boltz2/combininatorics_config.json" \
    "/runtime/001_Boltz2/queries.csv" \
    ...
```

In on-the-fly mode, `Pipeline._execute_tool_on_the_fly()` writes this script to disk, makes it executable, and invokes it via `subprocess.Popen` with line-buffered streaming — enabling real-time output visibility in notebooks while simultaneously writing to log files ([pipeline.py#L381-C404](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L381-L404)). If the process exits with a non-zero code, a `RuntimeError` is raised immediately.

> [!TIP]
> **HelpScripts are stateless** — they receive no in-memory Python objects. All context must be serialized to files (JSON, CSV, YAML) during configuration time and deserialized by the script at runtime. This is the fundamental constraint that enables cluster execution: any state an `execute`-mode user can create, a `save`-and-submit user can also reproduce.

> [!TIP]
> **Resolution scripts are the glue between bash loops and Python data structures.** When a generated bash script needs to iterate over DataStream IDs or look up per-item values, it calls `resolve_*.py` via command substitution rather than embedding Python logic inline. This keeps the generated bash script readable and the resolution logic centralized.

## Integration Pattern with BaseConfig

Every `BaseConfig` subclass that requires runtime processing declares HelpScript paths as `Path` descriptors. The `Boltz2` config exemplifies this pattern comprehensively:

```python
boltz_config_unified_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(
    self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_boltz_config_unified.py"))
boltz_postprocessing_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(
    self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_boltz_postprocessing.py"))
boltz_msa_copy_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(
    self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_boltz_msa_copy.py"))
```

These lazy-evaluated path descriptors resolve at script-generation time, after `set_pipeline_context()` has populated `self.folders`. The `generate_script()` method then interpolates these paths into the bash template, producing a self-contained execution script with no runtime dependency on the Python pipeline context.

Sources: [boltz2.py](biopipelines/boltz2.py#L101-L103), [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L437-L443)

## Package Import Convention

HelpScripts that need access to the `biopipelines` package use a consistent import bootstrap pattern — inserting the parent directory of `HelpScripts/` (i.e., the repository root) into `sys.path`:

```python
_biopipelines_dir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), '..', 'biopipelines')
sys.path.insert(0, _biopipelines_dir)
from biopipelines.combinatorics import predict_single_output_id
```

This allows HelpScripts to import from the framework's internal modules (`combinatorics`, `biopipelines_io`, `pdb_parser`, `sele_utils`) while remaining executable as standalone scripts outside any package context. The approach is deliberately redundant with proper package installation — it ensures scripts work even when `biopipelines` is not pip-installed, which is the common case during SLURM execution where scripts run from the repository checkout.

Sources: [pipe_boltz_config_unified.py](HelpScripts/pipe_boltz_config_unified.py#L30-L32), [pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py](HelpScripts/pipe_pmpnn_fixed_positions.py#L11-L13), [resolve_stream_ids.py](HelpScripts/resolve_stream_ids.py#L17-L19)

## Summary: HelpScripts as the Serialization Boundary

The HelpScripts layer is not an implementation detail — it is the **architectural serialization boundary** between biopipelines' rich Python configuration model and its bash-script execution model. By constraining all runtime computation to standalone CLI scripts that communicate exclusively through the filesystem, the framework achieves three critical properties: (1) **reproducibility** — every pipeline step is a deterministic function of input files and CLI arguments; (2) **portability** — the same bash scripts run identically on a laptop, a Jupyter notebook, or a SLURM cluster; and (3) **debuggability** — any pipeline step can be inspected, rerun, or modified by editing a single self-contained script in the `runtime/` folder.

For a deeper understanding of how HelpScripts are *generated* and *orchestrated*, see [Pipeline Orchestration Engine](18-helpscripts-runtime-layer). For the data structures that flow through these scripts, see [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container). For details on how tools define their script-generation logic, see [BaseConfig: Tool Abstraction Layer](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer).

# Jupyter Renderer System



The Jupyter Renderer System transforms raw pipeline output data into rich, interactive HTML visualizations directly within notebook cells. Rather than requiring separate plotting or inspection scripts, it leverages IPython's `_repr_html_()` display protocol so that any `ToolOutput` or `StandardizedOutput` object automatically renders as formatted HTML when it appears as the last expression in a cell. This system is the bridge between the pipeline's data layer — `DataStream` objects, `TableInfo` metadata, and file-based outputs — and the developer's visual inspection workflow.

## Rendering Architecture

The system follows a configuration-driven dispatch model. A central renderer registry in `config.yaml` maps stream formats and table names to Python scripts under `Renderers/`. When a `StandardizedOutput` needs to display itself, it loads the registry, matches each output stream or table to the appropriate renderer script, and calls the script's `render()` function to produce HTML fragments. These fragments are assembled with a shared CSS stylesheet into a single HTML string that the notebook frontend renders inline.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Jupyter Cell<br/>ToolOutput as last expression"] --> B["ToolOutput._repr_html_()"]
    B --> C["StandardizedOutput._repr_html_()"]
    C --> D{"Is notebook environment?"}
    D -- No --> E["Return None<br/>(plain __repr__)"]
    D -- Yes --> F["Load renderers config<br/>from config.yaml"]
    F --> G{"Tool has custom<br/>_repr_notebook_html?"}
    G -- Yes --> H["Use tool-specific<br/>visualization"]
    G -- No --> I["Dispatch to renderer scripts"]
    I --> J{"Stream or Table?"}
    J -- Stream --> K["Lookup: stream name → format → _default"]
    J -- Table --> L["Lookup: table name → _default"]
    K --> M["Render metadata + specialized renderer"]
    L --> N["Render table metadata + CSV content"]
    M --> O["Assemble HTML<br/>with shared CSS"]
    N --> O
    H --> O
    O --> P["IPython renders HTML<br/>in notebook cell"]
```

The entry point is `StandardizedOutput._repr_html_()` in [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1521-L1645). It first checks whether the code is running inside a notebook or Colab environment via `_is_notebook()` — if not, it returns `None` and IPython falls back to the plain-text `__repr__()`. Within a notebook, it loads the renderer configuration, iterates over all active streams and tables, dispatches each to the matched renderer, and concatenates the results.

Sources: [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1521-L1645), [config.yaml](config.yaml#L169-L188)

## Configuration and Dispatch Registry

Renderer mappings live under the `renderers` key in `config.yaml`. The configuration has two sections — `streams` and `tables` — each containing key-value pairs where keys are format identifiers or stream/table names, and values are paths to Python scripts relative to the repository root.

```yaml
renderers:
  streams:
    _metadata: Renderers/streams.py
    pdb: Renderers/structures.py
    cif: Renderers/structures.py
    "pdb|cif": Renderers/structures.py
    png: Renderers/images.py
    jpg: Renderers/images.py
    jpeg: Renderers/images.py
    svg: Renderers/images.py
    gif: Renderers/images.py
    bmp: Renderers/images.py
    tiff: Renderers/images.py
    webp: Renderers/images.py
    plots: Renderers/plots.py
    fasta: Renderers/fasta.py
    fa: Renderers/fasta.py
    _default: Renderers/streams.py
  tables:
    _default: Renderers/tables.py
```

The `_metadata` key plays a special role: when a specialized renderer is matched for a stream (e.g., `pdb` → `Renderers/structures.py`), the system first renders the stream's metadata using the `_metadata` script, then appends the specialized renderer's output. This ensures every stream always displays its summary table (name, format, item count, map_table) regardless of which visual renderer handles the data itself.

The lookup priority for streams follows a three-tier fallback: **stream name** → **format string** → **format.lower()** → **`_default`**. This means you can register a renderer by stream name (e.g., if a tool creates a stream named `plots`), by its format (e.g., `pdb`), or rely on the catch-all default. For tables, the lookup is simpler: **table name** → **`_default`**.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L169-L188), [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1489-L1520)

## Renderer Module Contract

Every renderer script under `Renderers/` must expose a top-level `render()` function with a consistent signature. The system loads these scripts dynamically using `importlib.util` and caches the loaded `render()` function in `StandardizedOutput._renderer_cache` to avoid redundant imports when the same renderer is invoked for multiple streams in a single cell output.

```python
# Renderer contract — every Renderers/*.py file must follow this pattern:
def render(stream_or_table_info, output):
    """
    Args:
        stream_or_table_info: DataStream (for stream renderers)
                              or TableInfo (for table renderers)
        output: StandardizedOutput — provides output_folder,
                rendering_parameters, and other context
    Returns:
        str — HTML fragment, or empty string / None to skip
    """
    ...
```

The renderer caching mechanism in `_load_render_fn()` resolves each script path to a module, extracts its `render` function, and stores it in the class-level `_renderer_cache` dictionary. Subsequent calls with the same path retrieve the cached function directly, which is critical when a notebook cell output contains many streams of the same format.

Sources: [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1476-L1488)

## Stream Renderers

### Default Metadata Renderer (`Renderers/streams.py`)

The default stream renderer serves two purposes: it acts as the `_metadata` pre-renderer for all streams, and it is the fallback visual renderer via the `_default` key. It produces a metadata table showing the stream's name, format, item count, map_table path, pattern status, and any metadata key-value pairs. Below the metadata, it renders the stream's actual data — either from the map_table CSV (if present) or as an id/file pairing table — using the same compact 2+…+2 row truncation pattern used across all table renderers.

The `_rel()` helper function in this renderer (and in `Renderers/tables.py`) converts absolute file paths to relative paths using the `<output_folder>/` prefix for cleaner display within notebook cells.

Sources: [Renderers/streams.py](Renderers/streams.py#L1-L109)

### 3D Structure Viewer (`Renderers/structures.py`)

The most feature-rich renderer in the system. It handles streams with formats `pdb`, `cif`, or the compound format `pdb|cif`, producing a fully interactive 3D molecular viewer powered by **py3Dmol** (loaded from a CDN). The renderer reads each structure file, embeds the atomic data as JSON literals directly in the generated JavaScript, and constructs a complete single-file HTML widget.

**Interactive controls** include a style toolbar with four molecular representations (cartoon, stick, sphere, surface), a ligand display toggle with three states (element coloring, pLDDT coloring, off), a spin toggle for continuous rotation, and navigation arrows for browsing through structures in the stream. Each structure also has a download button that creates a Blob URL for the current model's raw PDB/CIF text.

The viewer supports **pLDDT confidence coloring** for AlphaFold/Boltz predictions. When `rendering_parameters` on the output contain a `plddt_upper` value for the stream, the renderer activates a B-factor-based color function that maps residues to the standard AF confidence palette (blue ≥90%, cyan 70–90%, yellow 50–70%, orange <50%). A color legend is shown below the viewer when pLDDT mode is active. The pLDDT threshold scales linearly — a structure with `plddt_upper: 50` remaps the color boundaries proportionally, accommodating tools that normalize B-factors to different ranges.

Structures are capped at 50 items with a truncation notice, and format detection for `pdb|cif` streams inspects individual file extensions rather than assuming a uniform format across the entire stream.

Sources: [Renderers/structures.py](Renderers/structures.py#L8-L319)

### Image Renderer (`Renderers/images.py`)

Handles raster and vector image formats (png, jpg, jpeg, svg, gif, bmp, tiff, webp). For SVG files, it reads the raw markup and embeds it directly in the HTML, preserving scalability. For all other formats, it encodes the binary file contents as a base64 data URI with the appropriate MIME type (`image/png`, `image/jpeg`, etc.). Each image is displayed with its item ID as a caption above it, wrapped in a responsive container that constrains width to 100%.

Sources: [Renderers/images.py](Renderers/images.py#L1-L50)

### Plot Renderer (`Renderers/plots.py`)

A specialized renderer for plot-type streams. It reads each PNG image as base64 (like the generic image renderer) but adds a distinctive feature: it automatically discovers a **companion CSV file** at the same path with a `.csv` extension. If found, the CSV is parsed into a DataFrame and rendered as a compact HTML table alongside the plot image in a side-by-side flexbox layout — table on the left, image on the right. This layout is particularly useful for analysis tools like `Distance`, `Angle`, or `SequenceMetricCorrelation` that produce both a visualization and the underlying numerical data.

Sources: [Renderers/plots.py](Renderers/plots.py#L1-L101)

### FASTA Renderer (`Renderers/fasta.py`)

Renders FASTA sequence data as inline, colored, monospace sequence blocks following ClustalX conventions. The renderer parses the first valid FASTA file in the stream, auto-detects whether sequences are nucleotide or amino acid based on character composition, and applies the appropriate color palette. Amino acids are colored by property (hydrophobic = blue, positive = red, negative = magenta, polar = green, glycine = orange, proline = yellow, aromatic = cyan), while nucleotides use distinct colors for A, T/U, G, and C.

The display is capped at 50 sequences and 300 residues per line, with truncation notices where applicable. Gap characters (`-`, `.`) receive a neutral gray background. Sequence IDs are left-padded for alignment, creating a clean alignment-like visual block.

Sources: [Renderers/fasta.py](Renderers/fasta.py#L7-L140)

## Table Renderer (`Renderers/tables.py`)

The table renderer handles `TableInfo` objects (not `DataStream` objects). It renders a horizontal metadata row showing the table's name, path, column list, description, and row count, followed by the actual CSV content as an HTML table. Like the stream renderers, it uses the compact 2+…+2 row truncation pattern: when the table has more than 4 rows, only the first two and last two rows are displayed with an ellipsis row showing the count of hidden rows.

Sources: [Renderers/tables.py](Renderers/tables.py#L1-L87)

## Shared Visual Patterns

Several patterns recur across the renderer system and constitute its visual language:

**Compact truncation** is applied universally. Both stream data tables and table CSV content use the same algorithm: if the item count exceeds 4, display rows at indices 0, 1, n-2, n-1 with an ellipsis row after index 1 showing `"... N more ..."`. Individual cell values longer than 60 characters are truncated with `...` suffix.

**CSS class system** is centralized in `StandardizedOutput._CSS`. All renderers produce HTML using three CSS classes: `bp-table` for data tables (with alternating row backgrounds via `:nth-child(even)`), `bp-section` for top-level content blocks, and `bp-section-title` for section headings. The `bp-ellipsis` class styles truncation notice rows with italic gray text and centered alignment.

**Tool-specific override** is supported via a backward-compatibility hook. If a tool's `BaseConfig` subclass defines a `_repr_notebook_html(self, output)` method, the dispatch system calls it before the standard stream-by-stream rendering. If the method returns non-empty HTML, the entire standard rendering is skipped in favor of the tool's custom visualization. This allows individual tools to provide bespoke layouts — for example, a tool might want to render a specific matplotlib figure alongside its standard stream output.

Sources: [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1511-L1520), [Renderers/tables.py](Renderers/tables.py#L15-L47)

## Renderer Summary

| Renderer Script | Triggered By | Input Type | Output Format | Key Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Renderers/streams.py` | `_metadata`, `_default` | `DataStream` | Metadata + data table | Universal fallback for any stream |
| `Renderers/structures.py` | `pdb`, `cif`, `pdb\|cif` | `DataStream` | Interactive 3D widget | py3Dmol viewer with pLDDT coloring, navigation, download |
| `Renderers/images.py` | `png`, `jpg`, `jpeg`, `svg`, `gif`, `bmp`, `tiff`, `webp` | `DataStream` | Inline images | SVG passthrough, base64 raster, responsive layout |
| `Renderers/plots.py` | `plots` (by name) | `DataStream` | Image + companion CSV | Side-by-side plot/table layout |
| `Renderers/fasta.py` | `fasta`, `fa` | `DataStream` | Colored sequence block | ClustalX coloring, auto nucleotide/protein detection |
| `Renderers/tables.py` | `_default` | `TableInfo` | Metadata + CSV table | Named column display, compact truncation |

## Extending the Renderer System

To add a new renderer, create a Python file in `Renderers/` following the module contract (a `render(stream, output)` function returning HTML), then register it in `config.yaml` under the appropriate section. The key you choose determines when the renderer activates — use a format string like `sdf` to intercept all streams of that format, or a stream name to target a specific tool's output. Renderer scripts are loaded lazily and cached, so adding new renderers has no impact on startup performance for pipelines that don't produce the corresponding stream types.

For tools that require highly customized visualization — for instance, a tool that generates a multi-panel matplotlib figure combining structure overlays with scatter plots — the `_repr_notebook_html()` override on the tool's `BaseConfig` subclass provides full control over the HTML output, bypassing the standard dispatch entirely while still receiving the `StandardizedOutput` object for access to all stream and table data.

Sources: [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1582-L1591)

## Related Pages

The renderer system is the visual layer built on top of the data structures produced by pipeline execution. For understanding the data containers it renders, see [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container). For how outputs are produced and structured by tools, see [BaseConfig: Tool Abstraction Layer](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer). For the execution model that triggers output creation, see [Two-Phase Execution Model](9-two-phase-execution-model).

# Configuration Reference



This page provides a complete reference for every section of BioPipelines' `config.yaml`, the mechanism by which folder paths are resolved, and how the `ConfigManager` singleton connects the configuration file to tool environments and SLURM infrastructure. Understanding this file is essential for adapting BioPipelines to any compute environment — from a shared HPC cluster to a local workstation or Google Colab.

## Configuration Architecture

The configuration system follows a three-layer architecture: a **YAML file** declares all paths and settings, a **singleton `ConfigManager`** loads and validates it at runtime, and a **`FolderManager`** resolves the inter-dependent placeholder references into concrete absolute paths. Tools never read `config.yaml` directly — they receive a flat `folders` dictionary and an environment name through `BaseConfig`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["config.yaml"] -->|"load & validate"| B["ConfigManager<br/>(singleton)"]
    B -->|"folder_config"| C["FolderManager"]
    B -->|"environments"| D["BaseConfig._load_environments()"]
    B -->|"cluster settings"| E["Pipeline.slurm()"]
    B -->|"renderers"| F["StandardizedOutput._repr_html_()"]
    C -->|"placeholder resolution"| G["folders dict<br/>(flat key → absolute path)"]
    G -->|"injected into"| D
    G -->|"injected into"| E
```

## File Location and Selection Logic

`ConfigManager._get_config_path()` determines which configuration file to load using a priority system. On Google Colab, it first checks for `colab.yaml` in the repository root; if that exists, it is used instead of `config.yaml`. On all other environments, `config.yaml` is the sole configuration file. Both files reside at the repository root level.

Sources: [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L40-L63)

## Top-Level Sections

`config.yaml` contains six top-level sections. Only `folders` is strictly required — `ConfigManager` raises `ValueError` if it is missing. The remaining sections provide environment mappings, cluster settings, container paths, GNINA-specific runtime configuration, and Jupyter renderer mappings.

| Section | Required | Purpose |
|---------|----------|---------|
| `folders` | Yes | All filesystem path definitions with placeholder syntax |
| `environments` | No | Maps each `TOOL_NAME` to its conda/mamba environment |
| `cluster` | No | HPC deployment settings (email, env_manager, modules) |
| `containers` | No | Singularity/Apptainer image paths per tool |
| `gnina` | No | CUDA module and library path overrides for GNINA |
| `renderers` | No | Jupyter notebook display configuration per stream/table format |

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L1-L10), [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L89-L93)

## The `folders` Section

This is the core configuration section. It defines all filesystem paths used across the entire pipeline system using an ordered placeholder resolution scheme.

### Placeholder Syntax

Paths use angle-bracket placeholders to reference other folder keys. For example, `<home>` references the value of `folders.base.home`. At runtime, two special placeholders are injected before resolution begins: `<username>` resolves to the current system user (via `getpass.getuser()`), and `<cwd>` resolves to the repository root directory (parent of `biopipelines/` package).

Sources: [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L79-L91), [config.yaml](config.yaml#L15-L18)

### Resolution Order

`FolderManager` processes subsections in a strict order defined by `SECTION_ORDER`. Placeholders can only reference keys that were defined in an *earlier* section or in the same section (if the referenced key appears earlier within that section). The resolution order is:

1. **base** — fundamental paths (home, data, scratch, group, user, biopipelines, biopipelines_output)
2. **infrastructure** — shared resources (HelpScripts, PDBs, Ligands, Sequences, Tables, cache, containers)
3. **repositories** — tool installation directories (RFdiffusion, Boltz, AlphaFold, etc.)
4. **cache** — shared database/cache paths (BoltzCache, ColabFoldDatabases, MMseqs2Databases)
5. **derived** — computed paths (currently none in default config, reserved for user extensions)
6. **server** — runtime service paths (MMseqs2Server)

The `_resolve_path` method iteratively substitutes `<placeholder>` patterns up to 10 times per path to handle chained references like `<user>` → `<group>/<username>` → `<shares/locbp.chem.uzh>/<username>`, raising `FolderResolutionError` on circular references.

Sources: [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L30-L34), [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L93-L147)

### Runtime-Derived Paths

After config sections are resolved, `FolderManager._setup_runtime_paths()` creates four additional keys that depend on the pipeline's `project` and `job` arguments. These are not configurable via `config.yaml` — they are computed automatically:

| Key | Value |
|-----|-------|
| `project` | `<biopipelines_output>/<project>` |
| `output` | `<project>/<job>_NNN` (auto-incremented) |
| `runtime` | `<output>/RunTime` |
| `logs` | `<output>/Logs` |

Additionally, `job_id` is extracted from the output folder basename (the `NNN` suffix). When `local_output=True`, the `biopipelines_output` key is overridden to point to `./tests/` in the current working directory.

Sources: [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L149-L181)

### Default Configuration Reference

The following table documents every key in the default `folders` section, its template expression, and what it provides:

**base**

| Key | Template | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `home` | `/home/<username>` | User home directory |
| `data` | `<home>/data` | Local data storage for tool installations |
| `scratch` | `/scratch/<username>` | Temporary scratch storage |
| `group` | `/shares/locbp.chem.uzh` | Shared group storage |
| `user` | `<group>/<username>` | User directory on shared storage |
| `biopipelines` | `<cwd>` | Repository root |
| `biopipelines_output` | `<user>/BioPipelines` | Top-level output directory |

**infrastructure**

| Key | Template | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `HelpScripts` | `<biopipelines>/HelpScripts` | Helper Python/Bash scripts |
| `PDBs` | `<biopipelines>/PDBs` | Local PDB structure files |
| `Ligands` | `<biopipelines>/Ligands` | Local ligand files |
| `Sequences` | `<biopipelines>/Sequences` | Local sequence files |
| `Tables` | `<biopipelines>/Tables` | Local table (CSV/JSON) files |
| `cache` | `<group>/cache` | Shared cache directory |
| `containers` | `<group>/containers` | Singularity/Apptainer images |

**repositories**

| Key | Template | Tool |
|-----|----------|------|
| `RFdiffusion` | `<data>/RFdiffusion` | RFdiffusion |
| `RFdiffusionAllAtom` | `<data>/rf_diffusion_all_atom` | RFdiffusion All-Atom |
| `RFdiffusion3` | `<data>/rfdiffusion3` | RFdiffusion 3 |
| `ProteinMPNN` | `<data>/ProteinMPNN` | ProteinMPNN |
| `LigandMPNN` | `<data>/LigandMPNN` | LigandMPNN |
| `AlphaFold` | `<data>/localcolabfold` | AlphaFold (LocalColabFold) |
| `Boltz` | `<data>/boltz` | Boltz |
| `BoltzGen` | `<data>/boltzgen` | BoltzGen |
| `GhostFold` | `<data>/ghostfold` | GhostFold |
| `MMseqs2` | `<data>/mmseqs` | MMseqs2 |
| `ModelForge` | `<data>/modelforge` | ModelForge |
| `Gnina` | `<data>/gnina` | GNINA |

**cache**

| Key | Template | Description |
|-----|----------|-------------|
| `BoltzCache` | `<cache>/Boltz` | Boltz model cache |
| `BoltzGenCache` | `<cache>/BoltzGen` | BoltzGen model cache |
| `ColabFoldDatabases` | `<group>/models/colabfold_databases` | AlphaFold MSA databases |
| `MMseqs2Databases` | `<group>/models/mmseqs2_databases/gpu` | MMseqs2 search databases |

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L12-L49)

## The `environments` Section

This section maps each tool's `TOOL_NAME` to a conda/mamba environment name. When `BaseConfig.__init__` runs, it calls `_load_environments()`, which queries `ConfigManager.get_environment(self.TOOL_NAME)` to determine which environment to activate at script generation time. The lookup supports three forms per tool:

- **A string** (most common): `"Boltz2Env"` — single environment
- **A list**: `["dynamicbind", "relax"]` — multiple environments accessible via `activate_environment(index=N)`
- **Absent or `null`**: defaults to `"biopipelines"` in non-pip mode, or empty list in pip mode (e.g., Google Colab)

Sources: [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L195-L225), [config.yaml](config.yaml#L52-L105)

### Environment Reference by Category

| Category | Tool | Environment |
|----------|------|-------------|
| Structure Generation | RFdiffusion | `SE3nv` |
| Structure Generation | RFdiffusionAllAtom | `SE3nv` |
| Structure Generation | RFdiffusion3 | `foundry` |
| Structure Generation | BoltzGen / Merge / Import | `boltzgen` |
| Sequence Design | ProteinMPNN | `SE3nv` |
| Sequence Design | LigandMPNN | `ligandmpnn_env` |
| Sequence Design | MutationComposer / Mutagenesis | `MutationEnv` |
| Sequence Design | Fuse / StitchSequences / DNAEncoder | `biopipelines` |
| Structure Prediction | AlphaFold | `biopipelines` |
| Structure Prediction | GhostFold | `ghostfold` |
| Structure Prediction | Boltz2 | `Boltz2Env` |
| Structure Prediction | RF3 | `modelforge` |
| Flexibility | CABSflex | `CABSflex` |
| Analysis | Gnina / Distance / DistanceSelector | `biopipelines` |
| Analysis | ConformationalChange / Contacts / PoseChange / SASA | `ProteinEnv` |
| Analysis | MutationProfiler / SequenceMetricCorrelation / BayesianAdjuster | `MutationEnv` |
| Analysis | PoseBusters | `posebusters` |
| Data Management | Panda / ExtractMetrics | `biopipelines` |
| Data Management | Selection | `ProteinEnv` |
| Utilities | Load / MMseqs2 / CompoundLibrary / PDB / Sequence / Plot | `biopipelines` |
| Utilities | PyMOL | `ProteinEnv` |

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L52-L105)

## The `cluster` Section

This section controls HPC cluster deployment behavior and is consumed by `Pipeline.slurm()`, `ConfigManager.get_shell_hook_command()`, and related methods.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| `emails` | dict | `{}` | Maps Unix usernames to email addresses for SLURM notifications. Used with `Pipeline.slurm(email="auto")`. |
| `env_manager` | string | `mamba` | Environment manager command. Must be `"mamba"`, `"conda"`, or `"pip"`. Controls shell hook initialization (`eval "$(mamba shell.bash hook)"`) and activation commands. |
| `container_executor` | string | `apptainer` | Container runtime binary. Must be `"apptainer"` or `"singularity"`. |
| `slurm_modules` | list of strings | `["miniforge3", "apptainer"]` | Module commands loaded at the top of SLURM scripts via `module load ...`. Set to `[]` if your system has no module system. |

> [!TIP]
> The `env_manager` setting affects every generated script. When set to `"pip"`, `activate_environment()` returns a no-op comment and no shell hook is sourced — this is how Google Colab notebooks bypass environment management entirely. When set to `"conda"` or `"mamba"`, the appropriate shell hook and `activate` command are injected into every tool's script section.

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L112-L128), [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L155-L211)

## The `containers` Section

This section maps tool names to Singularity/Apptainer container image paths. When a container is configured for a tool, the pipeline uses it instead of the conda environment during script generation. Paths support the same `<placeholder>` syntax as the `folders` section and are resolved after all folder keys are available.

```yaml
containers:
  # Uncomment and adjust to enable containerized execution:
  # RFdiffusionAllAtom: "<RFdiffusionAllAtom>/rf_se3_diffusion.sif"
```

The `FolderManager._resolve_containers()` method processes this section after folder resolution. Container paths are then injected into the pipeline's `folders` dictionary with a `container:` prefix (e.g., `container:RFdiffusionAllAtom`).

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L131-L133), [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L101-L108), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L86-L88)

## The `gnina` Section

GNINA requires CUDA-specific modules and library paths that vary between HPC environments. This dedicated section stores those settings outside the generic `cluster` configuration.

| Key | Type | Description |
|-----|------|-------------|
| `modules` | list of strings | CUDA/cuDNN modules to load in the GNINA script section (e.g., `["cuda/12.6.3", "cudnn/9.8.0.87-12"]`) |
| `ld_library_path` | string | Value for `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` in the GNINA execution environment |

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L136-L139)

## The `renderers` Section

This section controls how tool outputs are displayed as rich HTML in Jupyter notebooks. It is consumed by `StandardizedOutput._repr_html_()` through `ConfigManager.get_renderers_config()`.

### Stream Renderers

Stream renderers are matched by a priority lookup: the stream's **name** is checked first, then its **file extension**, and finally the `_default` fallback.

| Key | Renderer Script | Handles |
|-----|----------------|---------|
| `_metadata` | `Renderers/streams.py` | Internal metadata streams |
| `pdb` | `Renderers/structures.py` | PDB structure files |
| `cif` | `Renderers/structures.py` | mmCIF structure files |
| `pdb\|cif` | `Renderers/structures.py` | Mixed structure streams |
| `png` / `jpg` / `jpeg` / `svg` / `gif` / `bmp` / `tiff` / `webp` | `Renderers/images.py` | Image files |
| `plots` | `Renderers/plots.py` | Matplotlib plot objects |
| `fasta` / `fa` | `Renderers/fasta.py` | FASTA sequence files |
| `_default` | `Renderers/streams.py` | Any unmatched stream format |

### Table Renderers

| Key | Renderer Script | Handles |
|-----|----------------|---------|
| `_default` | `Renderers/tables.py` | All table DataFrames |

Sources: [config.yaml](config.yaml#L142-L188), [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L1489-L1528)

## Tool-Level Configuration: Constructor Parameters

Beyond `config.yaml`, every tool accepts configuration parameters through its constructor. These are stored in `BaseConfig.params` during `__init__` and drive the tool's `generate_script()` output. The following table covers the common parameters inherited from `BaseConfig.__init__`:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `name` | string | `""` | Custom job name override. Propagates to SLURM `--job-name` and output file naming. |
| `pipeline` | Pipeline | `None` | Pipeline reference (set automatically in context-manager mode). |
| `resources` | dict | `{}` | Tool-specific resource overrides (`gpu`, `memory`, `time`, plus SLURM options). |
| `dependencies` | list | `[]` | Explicit dependency references to other tool configs. |

### Example: Boltz2 Constructor Parameters

Each tool defines its own specialized parameters beyond the base set. Boltz2, for instance, exposes over 20 parameters covering input sources, prediction behavior, template constraints, and post-processing options:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `config` | string | `None` | Pre-built configuration string |
| `proteins` | DataStream | `None` | Input protein structures |
| `ligands` | str/DataStream | `None` | Input ligand structures |
| `affinity` | bool | `True` | Compute binding affinity scores |
| `output_format` | string | `"pdb"` | Output structure format |
| `msa_server` | string | `"public"` | MSA generation server |
| `recycling_steps` | int | `None` | Override default recycling steps |
| `diffusion_samples` | int | `None` | Override default diffusion samples |
| `use_potentials` | bool | `False` | Enable potential-guided sampling |
| `template` | string | `None` | Template PDB path for constrained prediction |
| `pocket_residues` | list | `None` | Residue IDs defining the binding pocket |

Sources: [boltz2.py](biopipelines/boltz2.py#L106-L139), [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L162-L193)

## Pipeline-Level Configuration

The `Pipeline` constructor and its context-manager convenience functions provide runtime configuration that controls execution mode, resource allocation, and output naming.

### Pipeline Constructor

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `project` | string | — | Project name (top-level output folder) |
| `job` | string | — | Job name (auto-appends `_NNN` for uniqueness) |
| `description` | string | `"Description missing"` | Human-readable description |
| `on_the_fly` | bool/None | auto-detect | Execute tools immediately in Jupyter; auto-detects notebook environment |
| `local_output` | bool/None | follows `on_the_fly` | Write output to `./tests/` instead of configured path |

### Context-Manager Convenience Functions

These functions must be called inside a `with Pipeline(...)` block:

| Function | Parameters | Effect |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| `Resources(**kwargs)` | `gpu`, `memory`, `time`, plus SLURM options | Sets resource requirements for all subsequent tools until next `Resources()` call |
| `Suffix(suffix)` | `suffix: str` | Appends a suffix to tool folder names (e.g., `"001"`) |
| `Save()` | — | Saves pipeline script without submitting to SLURM |
| `Dependencies(job_ids)` | `job_ids: str or list` | Adds external SLURM job dependencies |

### GPU Specification Reference

The `gpu` parameter in `Resources()` accepts multiple formats that map to different SBATCH configurations:

| Value | SBATCH Effect |
|-------|---------------|
| `None` / `""` / `"none"` | No GPU allocation |
| `"T4"` / `"L4"` / `"V100"` / `"A100"` / `"H100"` / `"H200"` | `#SBATCH --gpus=<model>:1` |
| `"24GB"` / `"32GB"` / `"80GB"` / `"96GB"` | `#SBATCH --gpus=1` + memory constraint |
| `"32GB\|80GB\|96GB"` | OR-constraint combining multiple memory tiers |
| `"high-memory"` | Constraint: `GPUMEM32GB\|GPUMEM80GB\|GPUMEM96GB` |
| `"gpu"` / `"any"` | `#SBATCH --gpus=1` (no model constraint) |
| `"!L4"` | Excludes L4: `GPUMEM32GB\|GPUMEM80GB\|GPUMEM96GB` |

Sources: [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L50-L66), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L1421-L1541), [pipeline.py](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L660-L683)

## Path Descriptors: Lazy Evaluation in Tool Classes

Tools declare file paths as class-level `Path` descriptors that compute lazily — the path expression is only evaluated when first accessed, after `output_folder` and `folders` have been set by the pipeline. This pattern prevents errors from accessing paths before pipeline context is established.

```python
from biopipelines.file_paths import Path

class Boltz2(BaseConfig):
    # These resolve lazily after pipeline registration
    apo_config_folder = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "ApoConfig"))
    main_table = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "rfdiffusion_results.csv"))
    helper_script = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_boltz_config.py"))
```

The `Path` descriptor stores the result after first computation, so repeated access returns the cached value. This is used extensively across all tool classes — Boltz2 alone declares over 20 path descriptors for config files, output files, and helper scripts.

Sources: [file_paths.py](biopipelines/file_paths.py#L12-L41), [base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L45-L47), [boltz2.py](biopipelines/boltz2.py#L70-L104)

## Configuration Management API

The `ConfigManager` singleton exposes a programmatic API for accessing and manipulating the configuration at runtime. It also provides class methods for downloading and updating the config from the remote repository.

### Key Instance Methods

| Method | Returns | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `get_folder_config()` | `Dict[str, Any]` | Full `folders` section dictionary |
| `get_environment(tool_name)` | `Optional[str]` | Environment name for a specific tool |
| `get_all_environments()` | `Dict[str, Optional[str]]` | All tool → environment mappings |
| `get_env_manager()` | `str` | `"mamba"`, `"conda"`, or `"pip"` |
| `get_container_executor()` | `str` | `"apptainer"` or `"singularity"` |
| `get_container(tool_name)` | `Optional[str]` | Container path for a tool |
| `get_slurm_modules()` | `List[str]` | Module load list for SLURM scripts |
| `get_emails()` | `Dict[str, str]` | Username → email mapping |
| `get_shell_hook_command()` | `str` | Shell initialization command |
| `get_activate_command(env_name)` | `str` | Environment activation command |
| `get_module_load_line()` | `str` | Full `module load ...` line |
| `get_renderers_config()` | `Dict[str, Any]` | Stream and table renderer mappings |
| `reload()` | `None` | Re-reads `config.yaml` from disk |

### Key Class Methods

| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `ConfigManager.pull_config(force=False)` | Downloads config from GitHub; raises `FileExistsError` if exists and `force=False` |
| `ConfigManager.repull_config(backup=True)` | Backs up existing config and re-downloads |
| `ConfigManager.create_user_config()` | Auto-called when no config is found; attempts download |

> [!TIP]
> The `reload()` method is useful during interactive sessions. After editing `config.yaml`, calling `reload_config()` (the module-level convenience wrapper) forces the singleton to re-read the file, so subsequent tool instantiations pick up the changes without restarting the Python kernel.

Sources: [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L18-L337)

## Validation Rules

`ConfigManager._load_config()` enforces structural validation when loading `config.yaml`:

1. **Required sections**: The top-level `folders` key must exist, otherwise a `ValueError` is raised.
2. **Required folder subsections**: Within `folders`, the keys `base`, `infrastructure`, and `repositories` must all be present.
3. **YAML syntax**: Any YAML parsing error is caught and re-raised as `ValueError` with a descriptive message.
4. **Placeholder resolution**: `FolderManager` raises `FolderResolutionError` if any `<placeholder>` references a key that does not exist in the accumulated folder dictionary, or if circular references are detected (exceeding 10 iterations).

Sources: [config_manager.py](biopipelines/config_manager.py#L89-L107), [folders.py](biopipelines/folders.py#L110-L147)

## Next Steps

- **[BaseConfig: Tool Abstraction Layer](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer)** for how tools consume the configuration described on this page
- **[SLURM Cluster Integration](17-slurm-cluster-integration)** for end-to-end cluster deployment workflows using `Pipeline.slurm()`
- **[Custom Tool Development Guide](21-custom-tool-development-guide)** for defining new tools that integrate with the `Path` descriptor and environment system
- **[Google Colab Notebooks Guide](4-google-colab-notebooks-guide)** for how `colab.yaml` and `pip` mode simplify configuration on Colab

# Custom Tool Development Guide



This guide provides a complete reference for implementing new tools within the biopipelines framework. Every tool—whether it wraps an external binary, orchestrates a Python workflow, or performs pure data transformation—follows the same contract: subclass `BaseConfig`, implement four abstract methods, and declare outputs as `DataStream` and `TableInfo` objects. The framework handles pipeline registration, environment switching, script assembly, SLURM submission, and Jupyter rendering automatically.

## The Tool Contract: BaseConfig Anatomy

`BaseConfig` is the abstract root for every pipeline tool defined in [biopipelines/base_config.py](biopipelines/base_config.py#L34-L40). It establishes the lifecycle that all concrete tools must fulfill, from parameter validation through bash script generation to output declaration.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class BaseConfig {
        <<abstract>>
        +TOOL_NAME: str
        +pipeline_name: Path
        +log_file: Path
        +validate_params()* void
        +configure_inputs(pipeline_folders)* void
        +generate_script(script_path)* str
        +get_output_files()* Dict
        +_install_script(folders, env_manager) Optional~str~
        +get_config_display() List~str~
        +to_dict() Dict
    }
    
    class Path {
        <<descriptor>>
        +compute_fn: Callable
        +__get__(instance, owner) str
    }
    
    class DataStream {
        +name: str
        +ids: List~str~
        +files: List~str~
        +map_table: str
        +format: str
        +save_json(path) str
        +filter_by_ids(keep_ids) DataStream
    }
    
    class TableInfo {
        +name: str
        +path: str
        +columns: List~str~
        +info: TableMetadata
    }
    
    class RFdiffusion {
        +TOOL_NAME = "RFdiffusion"
        +generate_script() str
        +get_output_files() Dict
    }
    
    class PoseBusters {
        +TOOL_NAME = "PoseBusters"
        +generate_script() str
        +get_output_files() Dict
    }
    
    BaseConfig <|-- RFdiffusion
    BaseConfig <|-- PoseBusters
    BaseConfig --> Path : uses
    RFdiffusion --> DataStream : outputs
    RFdiffusion --> TableInfo : outputs
    PoseBusters --> TableInfo : outputs
```

The framework distinguishes two phases in every tool's lifecycle. The **configuration phase** runs in the Python process where you construct your pipeline: it validates parameters, resolves upstream dependencies, and declares expected outputs. The **execution phase** runs later on compute nodes via generated bash scripts: it activates conda environments, invokes external tools, and writes result tables and map files. Your tool class participates in both phases through different methods.

## Required Implementation: The Four Abstract Methods

Every tool must implement four abstract methods defined in `BaseConfig`. These form the minimal viable contract.

### `validate_params(self)`

Called during `__init__` ([base_config.py#L283-L285](biopipelines/base_config.py#L283-L285)). Validate all tool-specific parameters and raise `ValueError` with a descriptive message on failure. This runs before the tool is registered with any pipeline, ensuring early failure on misconfiguration.

```python
def validate_params(self):
    """Validate MyTool parameters."""
    if not self.structures_stream or len(self.structures_stream) == 0:
        raise ValueError("structures cannot be empty")
    if self.threshold < 0 or self.threshold > 1:
        raise ValueError("threshold must be between 0 and 1")
```

### `configure_inputs(self, pipeline_folders: Dict[str, str])`

Called by the pipeline after registration ([base_config.py#L341-L349](biopipelines/base_config.py#L341-L349)). Receives the resolved folder paths from `config.yaml` (e.g., `folders["HelpScripts"]`, `folders["data"]`). Store this reference—it's needed by `Path` descriptors and `generate_script`.

```python
def configure_inputs(self, pipeline_folders: Dict[str, str]):
    """Configure input structures."""
    self.folders = pipeline_folders
```

### `generate_script(self, script_path: str) -> str`

The most substantial method. Produces a bash script that will execute on the compute node ([base_config.py#L351-L362](biopipelines/base_config.py#L351-L362)). The canonical structure wraps your logic between the framework's completion-check header and footer, with environment activation in between.

### `get_output_files(self) -> Dict[str, List[str]]`

Declares what your tool produces ([base_config.py#L364-L372](biopipelines/base_config.py#L364-L372)). The return dictionary uses string keys for output streams (typically `"structures"`) and a `"tables"` key containing a dict of `TableInfo` objects, plus an `"output_folder"` key. This metadata drives downstream tool chaining and Jupyter rendering.

```python
def get_output_files(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    tables = {
        "my_results": TableInfo(
            name="my_results",
            path=self.results_csv,
            columns=["id", "score", "status"],
            description="MyTool analysis results",
            count=len(self.structures_stream)
        )
    }
    return {
        "structures": structures_datastream,
        "tables": tables,
        "output_folder": self.output_folder
    }
```

## Step-by-Step Tool Construction

The following flowchart shows the complete development process from file creation to pipeline integration.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Create biopipelines/my_tool.py] --> B[Subclass BaseConfig]
    B --> C[Set TOOL_NAME class attribute]
    C --> D[Define __init__ with parameters]
    D --> E[Declare Path descriptors for file paths]
    E --> F[Implement validate_params]
    F --> G[Implement configure_inputs]
    G --> H[Implement generate_script]
    H --> I[Implement get_output_files]
    I --> J["(Optional) Override _install_script"]
    J --> K["(Optional) Override get_config_display"]
    K --> L["(Optional) Override to_dict"]
    L --> M[Register tool in __init__.py]
    M --> N[Test in pipeline context]
```

### Step 1: Class Skeleton and `TOOL_NAME`

Create a new file in `biopipelines/` and subclass `BaseConfig`. The `TOOL_NAME` class attribute is the only required class-level declaration—it identifies the tool in folder naming (`NNN_ToolName/`), log files, and SLURM job names ([base_config.py#L42-L44](biopipelines/base_config.py#L42-L44)).

```python
from .base_config import BaseConfig, TableInfo
from .file_paths import Path
from .datastream import DataStream

class MyTool(BaseConfig):
    """One-line description of what the tool does."""
    
    TOOL_NAME = "MyTool"
```

### Step 2: Lazy Path Descriptors

The `Path` descriptor from [file_paths.py](biopipelines/file_paths.py#L12-L21) defers path computation until the `output_folder` and `folders` are available (set during `configure_inputs` via `set_pipeline_context`). Declare all file paths your tool needs—output files, helper scripts, intermediate configs—as class-level `Path` attributes.

```python
class MyTool(BaseConfig):
    TOOL_NAME = "MyTool"
    
    # Lazy path descriptors — resolved after configure_inputs
    results_csv = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "results.csv"))
    config_json = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "mytool_config.json"))
    helper_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_mytool.py"))
```

The `Path` descriptor is a Python descriptor that caches the computed path on first access. Its implementation in [file_paths.py#L22-L41](biopipelines/file_paths.py#L22-L41) stores the result on the instance, so subsequent accesses are O(1). This is critical because `output_folder` is not known at class definition time—it's injected by the pipeline when the tool is registered.

### Step 3: Constructor and Input Resolution

Your `__init__` should accept tool-specific parameters, resolve any `StandardizedOutput` or `DataStream` inputs to concrete `DataStream` objects, store the resolved state, and call `super().__init__(**kwargs)` last. The superclass constructor triggers `validate_params` and `_load_environments` ([base_config.py#L162-L193](biopipelines/base_config.py#L162-L193)).

The pattern for resolving upstream inputs is consistent across all existing tools. If a parameter accepts `Union[DataStream, StandardizedOutput]`, extract the appropriate stream from `StandardizedOutput` using its named attributes:

```python
def __init__(self,
             structures: Union[DataStream, StandardizedOutput],
             cutoff: float = 5.0,
             mode: str = "strict",
             **kwargs):
    # Resolve upstream input
    if isinstance(structures, StandardizedOutput):
        self.structures_stream = structures.streams.structures
    elif isinstance(structures, DataStream):
        self.structures_stream = structures
    else:
        raise ValueError(
            f"structures must be DataStream or StandardizedOutput, "
            f"got {type(structures)}"
        )
    
    self.cutoff = cutoff
    self.mode = mode
    super().__init__(**kwargs)
```

> [!TIP]
> Always call `super().__init__(**kwargs)` **last** in your constructor. The base class calls `validate_params()`, which requires all instance attributes to be set. Placing `super().__init__()` before attribute assignment will cause `AttributeError` in validation.

### Step 4: Script Generation

The `generate_script` method produces a complete bash script. The framework provides two helpers—`generate_completion_check_header()` and `generate_completion_check_footer()`—that wrap your logic in idempotency guards, preventing redundant execution on job resubmission ([base_config.py#L499-L555](biopipelines/base_config.py#L499-L555)).

The canonical script structure follows a consistent pattern visible in every tool implementation ([posebusters.py#L187-L195](biopipelines/posebusters.py#L187-L195), [rfdiffusion.py#L368-L383](biopipelines/rfdiffusion.py#L368-L383)):

```python
def generate_script(self, script_path: str) -> str:
    os.makedirs(self.output_folder, exist_ok=True)
    
    # 1. Serialize input DataStreams to JSON for runtime resolution
    self.structures_stream.save_json(self.input_json)
    
    script_content = "#!/bin/bash\n"
    script_content += "# MyTool execution script\n"
    
    # 2. Completion check header (skips if already done)
    script_content += self.generate_completion_check_header()
    
    # 3. Activate conda environment
    script_content += self.activate_environment()
    
    # 4. Write config JSON for the HelpScript to read
    config_data = {
        "structures_json": self.input_json,
        "cutoff": self.cutoff,
        "mode": self.mode,
        "output_csv": self.results_csv,
    }
    with open(self.config_json, 'w') as f:
        json.dump(config_data, f, indent=2)
    
    # 5. Tool-specific execution
    script_content += self._generate_run_section()
    
    # 6. Completion check footer (creates status file)
    script_content += self.generate_completion_check_footer()
    
    return script_content
```

> [!TIP]
> Always call `os.makedirs(self.output_folder, exist_ok=True)` at the top of `generate_script`. The output folder may not exist yet—especially during on-the-fly execution—and your serialized JSON configs must be written before the bash script runs.

### Step 5: Output Declaration via `get_output_files`

This method is called after `configure_inputs`, so all `Path` descriptors are resolvable. It must return a dictionary whose shape determines how downstream tools and the Jupyter renderer interact with your output ([posebusters.py#L236-L267](biopipelines/posebusters.py#L236-L267), [rfdiffusion.py#L445-L491](biopipelines/rfdiffusion.py#L445-L491)).

The return dictionary supports these optional keys:

| Key | Type | Description |
|-----|------|-------------|
| `"structures"` | `DataStream` | Output structure stream (PDB, CIF, SDF, etc.) |
| `"sequences"` | `DataStream` | Output sequence stream (FASTA, inline) |
| `"tables"` | `Dict[str, TableInfo]` | Named analysis tables with column metadata |
| `"output_folder"` | `str` | Path to this tool's output directory |

For tools that produce structures with pattern-based IDs (e.g., `["design_<0..9>"]`), use the `create_map_table` helper to generate the required `structures_map.csv`:

```python
def get_output_files(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    from .datastream import create_map_table
    from . import id_patterns
    
    # Pattern-based output IDs
    n = self.num_outputs
    structure_ids = [f"{self.pipeline_name}_<0..{n-1}>"]
    file_template = [os.path.join(self.output_folder, "<id>.pdb")]
    
    structures_map = os.path.join(self.output_folder, "structures_map.csv")
    create_map_table(
        structures_map,
        structure_ids,
        files=file_template
    )
    
    structures = DataStream(
        name="structures",
        ids=structure_ids,
        files=file_template,
        map_table=structures_map,
        format="pdb"
    )
    
    tables = {
        "results": TableInfo(
            name="results",
            path=self.results_csv,
            columns=["id", "score", "rank", "status"],
            description="MyTool generation results",
            count=n
        )
    }
    
    return {
        "structures": structures,
        "tables": tables,
        "output_folder": self.output_folder
    }
```

## Optional Overrides: Installation, Display, and Serialization

### Installation via `_install_script`

Override the classmethod `_install_script` to provide bash commands for setting up your tool's environment ([base_config.py#L61-L80](biopipelines/base_config.py#L61-L80)). Users call `MyTool.install()` within a pipeline context, which wraps your script in an `_Installer` step ([base_config.py#L693-L731](biopipelines/base_config.py#L693-L731)). The `force_reinstall` parameter lets users bypass idempotency checks.

```python
@classmethod
def _install_script(cls, folders, env_manager="mamba", force_reinstall=False, **kwargs):
    skip = "" if force_reinstall else """if {env_manager} env list 2>/dev/null | grep -q "mytool"; then
    echo "MyTool already installed, skipping."
    exit 0
fi
"""
    return f"""echo "=== Installing MyTool ==="
{skip}{env_manager} create -n mytool python=3.10 -y
{env_manager} activate mytool
pip install mytool-package

echo "=== MyTool installation complete ==="
"""
```

### Display Configuration via `get_config_display`

Override this method to add tool-specific lines to the pipeline summary output ([base_config.py#L466-L474](biopipelines/base_config.py#L466-L474)). Always call `super().get_config_display()` first, then append your lines.

```python
def get_config_display(self) -> List[str]:
    config_lines = super().get_config_display()
    config_lines.extend([
        f"STRUCTURES: {len(self.structures_stream)} files",
        f"CUTOFF: {self.cutoff}",
        f"MODE: {self.mode}",
    ])
    return config_lines
```

### Serialization via `to_dict`

Override `to_dict` to persist tool-specific parameters alongside the base configuration ([base_config.py#L483-L493](biopipelines/base_config.py#L483-L493)). This supports pipeline reproducibility and debugging.

```python
def to_dict(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    base_dict = super().to_dict()
    base_dict.update({
        "tool_params": {
            "cutoff": self.cutoff,
            "mode": self.mode,
        }
    })
    return base_dict
```

## HelpScripts: The Runtime Bridge

Most tools delegate their runtime logic to Python helper scripts in `HelpScripts/`. These scripts receive configuration via JSON files and perform the actual computation—file I/O, metric extraction, format conversion. The tool class serializes a config JSON in `generate_script`, then the bash script invokes the helper:

```
python {helper_py} --config {config_json}
```

This separation is architectural: the tool class operates in the configuration phase (pure Python, no heavy dependencies), while the HelpScript operates in the execution phase (full environment, arbitrary compute). The `Resolve.stream_item()` and `Resolve.stream_ids()` shell functions, available in every generated bash script, handle DataStream deserialization at runtime—translating JSON stream definitions into concrete file paths.

To create a new HelpScript, place it in `HelpScripts/pipe_mytool.py` and follow the `--config` pattern. Reference its path from your tool class using a `Path` descriptor:

```python
helper_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_mytool.py"))
```

## Complete Example: A Metric Extraction Tool

The following example demonstrates a tool that computes RMSD between structure pairs—an analysis tool with no external binary dependency, only a HelpScript.

```python
import os, json
from typing import Dict, List, Any, Optional, Union

from .base_config import BaseConfig, TableInfo
from .file_paths import Path
from .datastream import DataStream


class RMSDAnalyzer(BaseConfig):
    """Compute pairwise RMSD between predicted and reference structures."""

    TOOL_NAME = "RMSDAnalyzer"

    @classmethod
    def _install_script(cls, folders, env_manager="mamba",
                        force_reinstall=False, **kwargs):
        # No external tools needed — biopipelines env suffices
        return None

    # Lazy path descriptors
    results_csv = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "rmsd.csv"))
    config_json = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(self.output_folder, "rmsd_config.json"))
    rmsd_py = Path(lambda self: os.path.join(
        self.folders["HelpScripts"], "pipe_rmsd.py"))

    def __init__(self,
                 predicted: Union[DataStream, 'StandardizedOutput'],
                 reference: Union[DataStream, 'StandardizedOutput'],
                 method: str = "ca",
                 **kwargs):
        if isinstance(predicted, StandardizedOutput):
            self.predicted_stream = predicted.streams.structures
        elif isinstance(predicted, DataStream):
            self.predicted_stream = predicted
        else:
            raise ValueError(
                f"predicted must be DataStream or StandardizedOutput")

        if isinstance(reference, StandardizedOutput):
            self.reference_stream = reference.streams.structures
        elif isinstance(reference, DataStream):
            self.reference_stream = reference
        else:
            raise ValueError(
                f"reference must be DataStream or StandardizedOutput")

        self.method = method
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

    def validate_params(self):
        if self.method not in ("ca", "all", "bb"):
            raise ValueError(
                f"method must be 'ca', 'all', or 'bb', got '{self.method}'")
        if len(self.predicted_stream) != len(self.reference_stream):
            raise ValueError(
                "predicted and reference must have the same number of items")

    def configure_inputs(self, pipeline_folders: Dict[str, str]):
        self.folders = pipeline_folders

    def get_config_display(self) -> List[str]:
        lines = super().get_config_display()
        lines.extend([
            f"PREDICTED: {len(self.predicted_stream)} structures",
            f"REFERENCE: {len(self.reference_stream)} structures",
            f"METHOD: {self.method}",
        ])
        return lines

    def generate_script(self, script_path: str) -> str:
        os.makedirs(self.output_folder, exist_ok=True)

        self.predicted_stream.save_json(
            os.path.join(self.output_folder, "predicted.json"))
        self.reference_stream.save_json(
            os.path.join(self.output_folder, "reference.json"))

        config = {
            "predicted_json": os.path.join(
                self.output_folder, "predicted.json"),
            "reference_json": os.path.join(
                self.output_folder, "reference.json"),
            "method": self.method,
            "output_csv": self.results_csv,
        }
        with open(self.config_json, 'w') as f:
            json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

        script = "#!/bin/bash\n"
        script += self.generate_completion_check_header()
        script += self.activate_environment()
        script += f'python "{self.rmsd_py}" --config "{self.config_json}"\n'
        script += self.generate_completion_check_footer()
        return script

    def get_output_files(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        tables = {
            "rmsd": TableInfo(
                name="rmsd",
                path=self.results_csv,
                columns=["id", "predicted", "reference", "rmsd", "method"],
                description=f"RMSD analysis ({self.method})",
                count=len(self.predicted_stream),
            )
        }
        return {
            "tables": tables,
            "output_folder": self.output_folder,
        }

    def to_dict(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        d = super().to_dict()
        d["tool_params"] = {"method": self.method}
        return d
```

## Tool Registration and Use

After creating your tool file, register it in `biopipelines/__init__.py` so it's importable. Then use it within any pipeline context—auto-registration via `__new__` means simply constructing the tool inside a `with Pipeline(...)` block is sufficient ([base_config.py#L117-L160](biopipelines/base_config.py#L117-L160), [pipeline.py#L277-L345](biopipelines/pipeline.py#L277-L345)):

```python
from biopipelines import Pipeline, RMSDAnalyzer, Boltz2, AlphaFold

with Pipeline("rmsd_analysis", "test", "Compare predictions") as p:
    sequences = Sequence(seq="")

    predicted = Boltz2(proteins=sequences, num_designs=5)
    reference = AlphaFold(proteins=sequences)
    
    results = RMSDAnalyzer(predicted=predicted, reference=reference, method="ca")
    
    # Access results
    print(results.tables.rmsd.info.path)  # Table path
```

## Checklist: From Concept to Production

| Step | Requirement | Verified By |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| 1 | Subclass `BaseConfig` | `class MyTool(BaseConfig)` |
| 2 | Set `TOOL_NAME` | Class attribute string |
| 3 | Declare `Path` descriptors | All file paths are lazy |
| 4 | Resolve `StandardizedOutput` → `DataStream` | In `__init__` |
| 5 | Call `super().__init__(**kwargs)` last | Triggers validation |
| 6 | Implement `validate_params` | Raises `ValueError` on bad input |
| 7 | Implement `configure_inputs` | Stores `self.folders` |
| 8 | Implement `generate_script` | Header + env + logic + footer |
| 9 | Implement `get_output_files` | Returns streams + tables dict |
| 10 | Create HelpScript | In `HelpScripts/pipe_mytool.py` |
| 11 | Register in `__init__.py` | Importable from `biopipelines` |
| 12 | Test in pipeline context | Auto-registration works |

For deeper understanding of the mechanisms this guide builds upon, see [BaseConfig: Tool Abstraction Layer](8-baseconfig-tool-abstraction-layer), [Two-Phase Execution Model](9-two-phase-execution-model), and [DataStream: Unified I/O Container](7-datastream-unified-i-o-container). For SLURM resource configuration relevant to your tool's compute requirements, see [SLURM Cluster Integration](17-slurm-cluster-integration).
